passages.title: All He owns, all He knows
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat open the surah by placing everything that exists inside two circles: what Allah **owns**, and what Allah **knows**. Ayah 1 declares that all praise belongs to Him because all that is in the heavens and the earth is His — in this life and in the next. Ayah 2 then shows that His ownership is not a distant title but an intimate awareness: nothing sinks into the soil, sprouts out of it, comes down from the sky, or climbs up to it outside His knowledge. Four divine names close the two ayat — All-Wise, All-Aware, Most Merciful, Oft-Forgiving — and they are the hinge that holds the passage together.

## "All praise is due to Allah" — and why

The opening is not simply an act of praise; it comes with its reason attached. Ibn Kathir explains that Allah tells us **all praise belongs to Him alone in this world and in the Hereafter, because He is the Giver and Bestower** who gives to the people of this world and the people of the Hereafter, **the Sovereign and Controller of all**.

That is worth pausing over. Praise (*ḥamd*) here is not flattery offered to a powerful being. On Ibn Kathir's reading it is the fitting response to something already true: whatever the people of this world hold, and whatever the people of the Hereafter will hold, came from the Giver and Bestower. So praise is not something we generously give Allah; it is His by right, in the same way that what is in the heavens and the earth is His by right.

Ibn Kathir brings two other ayat alongside this one to bring out the point:

> "And He is Allah; none has the right to be worshipped but He, all praise is due to Him (both) in the first (i.e., in this world) and in the last (the Hereafter). And for Him is the decision, and to Him shall you (all) be returned." (28:70)

> "And truly, unto Us (belong) the last (Hereafter) and the first (this world)." (92:13)

Both worlds, both praises — one Owner.

## What "belongs to Him" actually means

The phrase in ayah 1 — *lahu mā fī s-samāwāti wa mā fī l-arḍ*, "to Whom belongs all that is in the heavens and all that is in the earth" — could be read thinly, as though it described a legal title with no consequences. Ibn Kathir closes that door. He glosses it: **"all of it is His dominion and is enslaved by Him and subject to His control."**

Three ideas, stacked. *Dominion* — it is His property, not on loan from anyone. *Enslaved by Him* — created things stand before Him as a servant stands before his Master. *Subject to His control* — nothing in the heavens or the earth is outside His disposal. And note the word Ibn Kathir chooses to begin with: **all** of it. The gloss admits no exception.

## "His is all praise in the Hereafter"

Why say it twice? Ayah 1 has already given Him the praise of both realms by naming Him Owner of all. Then it adds explicitly: *wa lahu l-ḥamdu fī l-ākhirah* — "His is all praise in the Hereafter."

Ibn Kathir's comment is short and immense: **"for He is the One Who will be worshipped forever and praised for eternity."**

Two words in that line carry the weight: *forever* and *for eternity*. The praise being spoken of has no end point. For a reader living in the middle of a noisy, distracted world, that is quietly steadying. The praise you offer now — halting, small, easily forgotten — is directed to the One who will be worshipped and praised without end.

## Two names: al-Ḥakīm and al-Khabīr

Ayah 1 closes: *wa huwa l-Ḥakīmu l-Khabīr* — "and He is the All-Wise, the All-Aware."

**al-Ḥakīm, the All-Wise.** Ibn Kathir explains this as wisdom **"in all that He says and does, legislates and decrees."** That covers four arenas at once: His speech, His acts, His law, and His decree. So the wisdom claimed here is not only that Allah designed the world well. It is also that His commands are wise — what He legislates is wise legislation — and that what He decrees is wise decree. Ibn Kathir's list places "decrees" alongside "legislates" without qualification, which means the decree a believer cannot make sense of is included in the wisdom, not exempted from it. A believer who has internalised *al-Ḥakīm* does not need to understand a decree in order to trust it.

**al-Khabīr, the All-Aware.** Ibn Kathir defines it by what it excludes: **"from Whom nothing at all is hidden or concealed."** Not partly known, not mostly known — nothing at all is out of view.

Ibn Kathir then cites an elegant early comment: **Malik narrated that az-Zuhri said, "He is All-Aware of His creation, All-Wise in His commands."** (This is a saying of az-Zuhri, an early scholar, transmitted by Malik — not a statement of the Prophet ﷺ.) That single line pairs the two names with two objects. His awareness faces His creation — He knows what He has made. His wisdom faces His commands — what He orders is placed with perfect judgement. Read that way, the two names are not a decorative flourish at the end of the ayah; they are the bridge into ayah 2, which is nothing but a demonstration of *al-Khabīr* in action.

A note on how we hold these names. This is our own creed rather than a line from the commentary: as Ahl al-Sunnah we affirm the attributes these names carry — wisdom, awareness, mercy, forgiveness — as real attributes of Allah, in the way He affirms them for Himself, without imagining them to resemble the wisdom or awareness of creatures, and without emptying them of meaning as though they were only figures of speech.

## Ayah 2: four movements, one knowledge

Ayah 2 takes the vast claim of ayah 1 and makes it tangible by naming four movements:

1. **What goes into the earth** — *mā yaliju fī l-arḍ*
2. **What comes forth from it** — *mā yakhruju minhā*
3. **What descends from the heaven** — *mā yanzilu mina s-samāʾ*
4. **What ascends into it** — *mā yaʿruju fīhā*

Down into the earth, up out of it; down from the sky, up to the sky. Each of the two realms named in ayah 1 — the heavens and the earth — is traced in both directions. And the name that just preceded this list tells us how to read it: He is the One **from Whom nothing at all is hidden or concealed**.

**Into the earth and out of it.** Ibn Kathir fills this in with striking concreteness: **He knows the number of raindrops that sink into the depths of the earth, and the seeds that have been sown, and the things that are hidden in it** — and then He knows **what comes forth from that, how many they are, how they grow and what they look like.**

Sit with that. Not "He knows that rain falls" but *the number* of drops, each one tracked down into the dark. Not "He knows that plants grow" but the count of what emerges, the manner of its growing, and its appearance. Ibn Kathir's own phrase for what goes down is "the things that are hidden in it" — so this is knowledge of exactly what no human observer is positioned to see.

**Down from the sky and up to it.** Ibn Kathir glosses what descends as **"raindrops and provision"**, and what ascends as **"righteous deeds and other things."**

That pairing is the heart of the passage. What comes down is *rizq* — provision, the water and sustenance that keep creatures alive. What goes up includes *ʿamal ṣāliḥ* — righteous deeds; Ibn Kathir adds "and other things," so he does not limit the upward traffic to deeds alone. But it is worth noticing what he names first in each direction: provision descending, righteous deeds ascending.

And it reframes worship. Your prayer in an empty room, the charity nobody saw, the tongue you held when you wanted to answer back — Ibn Kathir places righteous deeds among what *ascends*, and the One who receives them is the One who knows the number of the raindrops going down.

## The names that close it: ar-Raḥīm and al-Ghafūr

Ayah 2 could have ended by hammering the point home with a name of power or reckoning. Instead it ends: *wa huwa r-Raḥīmu l-Ghafūr* — "And He is the Most Merciful, the Oft-Forgiving."

Ibn Kathir explains: **He is Most Merciful to His servants; He does not hasten to punish them, and He forgives the sins of those who repent to Him and put their trust in Him.**

This is where the passage becomes personal, and it is the reason the two ayat belong together as one unit. Ayah 1 says: everything is His. Ayah 2 says: and nothing at all is hidden or concealed from Him. Taken alone, that could be read as a total Owner with total awareness and nothing more. But the ayah does not stop there. The One from whom nothing is concealed is *ar-Raḥīm*, and Ibn Kathir spells out what that mercy looks like in practice: **He does not hasten to punish**. The delay is not a gap in His knowledge; Ibn Kathir names it as mercy.

And He is *al-Ghafūr* — He forgives, and Ibn Kathir's wording names two things about those He forgives: **they repent to Him, and they put their trust in Him.** Repentance is the turning back; trust is the confidence that turning back will be received. Both appear in the description, which is worth noticing, because a person can be sorry and still not believe that forgiveness is available to *him*.

## Living it

Read as a whole, these two ayat quietly rearrange how a believer stands in the world.

**Praise as the default, not the exception.** If all of it is His dominion, and He is the Giver and Bestower to the people of this world and the Hereafter, then praise is not an occasional religious mood; it is the accurate description of your situation.

**Trust where you cannot see.** He is All-Wise in what He decrees as much as in what He legislates — Ibn Kathir lists them together. The decree you do not understand is not outside that wisdom.

**Nothing hidden is unseen, and deeds do not stay where they happen.** He knows the number of the drops that sink into the depths of the earth, and He knows the things hidden in it. Righteous deeds are among what ascends — so work in secret with confidence, and let go of secret sin, since nothing at all was ever concealed from Him.

**Do not read His patience as indifference.** He does not hasten to punish, and He forgives those who repent to Him and put their trust in Him. That is not a loophole in the passage; it is how the passage chooses to end.

passages.title: Denying the Hour, and its two outcomes
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat take a single flat denial from the disbelievers — "The Hour will never come to us" — and answer it completely: first with an oath, then with the attribute of Allah that dismantles their objection, then with the two outcomes that make the Hour necessary in the first place, and finally with the testimony of those who were given knowledge. What holds the passage together is that one denial and its full reply. Ayah 3 is the answer; ayat 4 and 5 give the *reason* the Hour must come; ayah 6 shows what the whole thing looks like to people who were given knowledge.

## "The Hour will not come to us"

Notice the shape of their claim in ayah 3. They do not say *the Hour is unlikely*. They say **لَا تَأْتِينَا السَّاعَةُ** — "it will not come to *us*." And the reply the Prophet ﷺ is given is not an argument but an oath: **قُلْ بَلَىٰ وَرَبِّي لَتَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ** — *"Say: 'Yes, by my Lord, it will come to you…'"*

Ibn Kathir points out something striking about this oath:

> "This is one of three Ayat – there is no fourth – where Allah commands His Messenger ﷺ to swear by His Almighty Lord that the resurrection will surely come, because the stubborn followers of disbelief denied that it would happen."

The three, as he lists them:

1. **Sūrah Yūnus** — *"And they ask you to inform them (saying): 'Is it true?' Say: 'Yes! By my Lord! It is the very truth! and you cannot escape it!'"* (10:53)
2. **This ayah** — *"Those who disbelieve say: 'The Hour will not come to us.' Say: 'Yes, by my Lord, it will come to you…'"* (34:3)
3. **Sūrat at-Taghābun** — *"The disbelievers pretend that they will never be resurrected (for reckoning). Say: 'Yes! By my Lord, you will certainly be resurrected, then you will be informed of what you did; and that is easy for Allah'"* (64:7)

Three times in the entire Qur'an the Messenger ﷺ is told to *swear* — and all three times the subject is the same: the resurrection. That tells you how central this one truth is. And Ibn Kathir gives the reason plainly: the denial was not a sincere question but the settled position of "the stubborn followers of disbelief." To a refusal that hardened, Allah has His Prophet ﷺ stake an oath in his Lord's name.

## Why "the Knower of the Unseen"?

The oath does not end at "by my Lord." Allah is then described in a way that answers the denial directly:

> **عَالِمِ الْغَيْبِ ۖ لَا يَعْزُبُ عَنْهُ مِثْقَالُ ذَرَّةٍ فِي السَّمَاوَاتِ وَلَا فِي الْأَرْضِ وَلَا أَصْغَرُ مِنْ ذَٰلِكَ وَلَا أَكْبَرُ إِلَّا فِي كِتَابٍ مُبِينٍ**
>
> "the All-Knower of the Unseen, not even the weight of a speck of dust or less than that or greater escapes His knowledge in the heavens or in the earth but it is in a Clear Book."

Ibn Kathir notes that Allah here "is described in a manner that affirms" the oath — that is, this description is not a decoration on the end of the sentence; it is what establishes the point.

**Maʿārif ul Qurʼān** asks why *this* attribute, and answers with becoming caution:

> "At this place, out of the many attributes of Allah Taʿālā, the attribute of all-encompassing knowledge and the knowledge of the unseen has, perhaps, been mentioned particularly because the text is dealing with the matter of the deniers of the day of Resurrection."

Then it lays out what those deniers were actually thinking:

> "The major reason why the disbelievers rejected the inevitability of Qiyamah, the day of doom, was their inability to comprehend how the whole thing would work out."

Follow the reasoning as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān traces it. Human beings die and become dust; the particles of that dust are scattered all over the world. So — they wondered — how would it be possible to collect all those particles, separate the particles belonging to each human being from the particles of all others, and then put the relevant particles back into the frame of everyone's existence? The task looked impossible to them.

And then comes the diagnosis of their error:

> "they took it as impossible because they had very conveniently taken the knowledge and power of Allah Taʿālā on the analogy of their own knowledge and power!"

That is the whole mistake in one line. They measured Allah by themselves. *We* could not track those particles, therefore it cannot be done. The reply of the ayah is not to make the task sound easier — it is to correct the measure. Allah's knowledge "encompasses the entire universe in a manner that He knows everything in the heavens and the earth to the extent that He also knows where and in what state it is. Not a single particle of what has been created remains outside His knowledge."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then adds a boundary that matters for our creed: this comprehensive and all-encompassing knowledge "is hallmark of Allah Taʿālā. No created entity, whether an angel or prophet, can ever have such an all-encompassing knowledge that no particle of this universe remains outside it." Knowledge of the unseen in this absolute sense belongs to Allah alone; the angels and the prophets, however honoured, know what Allah gives them to know.

And so the conclusion writes itself: "for a Being that has such an all-encompassing knowledge, why would it be difficult to reclaim the scattered particles of a human being from all over the universe, each separate from the other, and reconstitute their bodies from these once again?"

Ibn Kathir makes the same move in his own words: "Even though bones may be scattered and disintegrate, He knows where they have gone and where they have dispersed, then He will bring them back just as He created them in the first place, because He has knowledge of all things." He also reports two of the early authorities on the phrase — **Mujāhid and Qatādah** said simply: *"Nothing is hidden or concealed from Him."*

**A note on the weight of a speck.** The ayah does not stop at "the weight of a speck of dust." It reaches in both directions — "less than that or greater" — and it locates all of it in a **كِتَابٍ مُبِينٍ**, a *Clear Book*. As Ibn Kathir puts it, "everything is encompassed by His knowledge, and nothing is hidden from Him."

## Ayah 4: why the Hour must come at all

Having established that resurrection is *possible*, ayat 4 and 5 say why it is *necessary*. Ibn Kathir introduces them as Allah telling us "of His wisdom in re-creating bodies and bringing about the Hour."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the connection back: **لِيَجْزِيَ** ("so that He rewards those who believed") in ayah 4 is joined to **لَتَأْتِيَنَّكُمْ** in ayah 3 — "al-Qiyāmah or the Doomsday is bound to come and its purpose will be to reward believers and to provide for them the best sustenance from Jannah (Paradise)." The Hour is not an arbitrary catastrophe. It has a purpose, and the purpose is a reckoning.

And the reward the ayah names for those who "believe and do righteous good deeds" comes in two words: **مَغْفِرَةٌ** — forgiveness — and **رِزْقٌ كَرِيمٌ**, "generous provision." Ibn Kathir sums up what this half of the pair means: "He will bestow His favor upon the blessed, who are the believers."

## Ayah 5: striving to make Allah fail

Now the other outcome. **وَالَّذِينَ سَعَوْا فِي آيَاتِنَا مُعَاجِزِينَ** — "those who strive against Our Ayat to frustrate them."

Ibn Kathir reads this as "those who try to turn others away from the path of Allah and who disbelieve His Messengers." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is more specific still: they are "those who made efforts to find faults with Our verses and tried to stop people from believing in them." So this is not simple unbelief sitting quietly at home. Both readings describe *effort* — "those who made efforts," in Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's rendering. They worked at it: picking at the revelation for flaws, and working on other people to keep them away from it.

Then the word that gives the ayah its edge: **مُعَاجِزِينَ**. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains it as meaning "that this effort by them was as if they would render Us helpless in seizing them and would thus go scot-free from having to be present on the last day of Qiyāmah."

That is worth sitting with. Their whole posture — arguing the Hour away, keeping others from it — was, on this reading, an attempt to slip out of the appointment altogether, as though Allah could be left unable to seize them. It fails.

Their outcome: **عَذَابٌ مِنْ رِجْزٍ أَلِيمٌ** — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: "these people shall receive punishment, a severe punishment that will be painful." Ibn Kathir sums up the pair of ayat: "He will bestow His favor upon the blessed, who are the believers, and will punish the doomed, who are the disbelievers."

## The two outcomes cannot be one outcome

Ibn Kathir supports this division with two other passages:

> "Not equal are the dwellers of the Fire and the dwellers of the Paradise. It is the dwellers of Paradise that will be successful." (59:20)

> "Shall We treat those who believe and do righteous good deeds like those who cause mischief on the earth? Or shall We treat those who have Taqwa as the evildoers?" (38:28)

Both are questions with only one possible answer, and both bear on ayat 4 and 5. The believer who did righteous deeds and the man who spent his life picking at revelation and blocking people from it are not equal, and will not be treated as equal. That is precisely the "wisdom" Ibn Kathir says these ayat disclose: the Hour is where the difference between the two is made plain. So the denial in ayah 3 is not only a mistake about Allah's knowledge and power; it is, in effect, a claim that nothing will ever be sorted out. The Hour is the answer to that too.

## Ayah 6: knowledge that becomes sight

Ayah 6 turns to a third group — neither the deniers nor an abstract audience, but **الَّذِينَ أُوتُوا الْعِلْمَ**, "those who have been given knowledge." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies them as the believers, spoken of here "in contrast with those who denied the coming of the Qiyāmah": they "had put their faith in it and became the beneficiaries of the knowledge given by Allah Taʿālā to the Holy Prophet ﷺ by revelation." Their knowledge is not something they generated — as the ayah's own wording says, they *have been given* it, and it came down through revelation.

Ibn Kathir calls this "another kind of wisdom, following on from the one before." Here is his picture of the moment:

> "when those who believed in what was revealed to the Messengers see the onset of the Hour and how the righteous and the wicked will be rewarded and punished respectively, which they knew of beforehand in this world from the Books of Allah and which they are now seeing with their own eyes…"

That is the wisdom: what they had accepted on the authority of the Books of Allah they now *watch happen*. The ayah says they **see** — and Ibn Kathir's phrase is exact: "now seeing with their own eyes." What was faith becomes eyesight, and nothing about the content changes; only their relationship to it does.

And on that day they speak. Ibn Kathir gathers the words for that moment:

> "Indeed, the Messengers of our Lord did come with the truth" (7:43)

> "This is what the Most Gracious had promised, and the Messengers spoke truth!" (36:52)

> "Indeed you have stayed according to the decree of Allah, until the Day of Resurrection; so this is the Day of Resurrection" (30:56)

The first two are outright vindications of the messengers; the third is the recognition that the appointed Day has in fact arrived. That is the answer to the denial with which the passage opened: what was revealed to the Prophet ﷺ "from your Lord is the truth," and there will be a day when the people of knowledge say so out loud with the thing itself in front of their eyes.

## "The Exalted in Might, the Owner of all praise"

The passage ends by naming where that revelation leads: **وَيَهْدِي إِلَىٰ صِرَاطِ الْعَزِيزِ الْحَمِيدِ** — "and that it guides to the path of the Exalted in might, Owner of all praise." Ibn Kathir defines both names:

**الْعَزِيز (al-ʿAzīz), the Exalted in Might** — "the One Who is All-Powerful, Whom none can overwhelm or resist, but He subjugates and controls all things."

**الْحَمِيد (al-Ḥamīd), the Owner of All Praise** — "the One Who, in all His words, deeds, laws and decrees, is deserving of praise, may He be glorified and exalted."

For a reader who has just come through ayah 5, these two definitions are worth sitting with. One tells us that none can overwhelm or resist Him. The other tells us that in all His words, deeds, laws and decrees He is deserving of praise. The Hour, on this ending, is the act of One who cannot be resisted and who is never blameworthy in what He does.

## Living it

**Stop measuring Allah by yourself.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān put its finger on the exact root of the denial: taking "the knowledge and power of Allah Taʿālā on the analogy of their own knowledge and power." That instinct is not confined to disbelievers. Whenever we quietly decide something is too far gone to be repaired, too long past to be recorded, too small to have registered — we are doing the same arithmetic. The ayah answers it: not the weight of a speck of dust, nor anything less or greater, escapes His knowledge, and all of it is in a Clear Book.

**Take the record seriously.** If nothing is hidden or concealed from Him, as Mujāhid and Qatādah said, and everything is in that Clear Book, then the small good deed nobody noticed is on the page, and so is the small wrong we assumed was too minor to count.

**Aim at the two words of ayah 4.** Forgiveness, and generous provision — and belief with righteous deeds is what the ayah names as the road to them. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the purpose of that Day for such people as "to reward believers and to provide for them the best sustenance from Jannah."

**Note which truth was given an oath.** Ibn Kathir counts three ayat — "there is no fourth" — where the Prophet ﷺ is commanded to swear by his Lord, and all three concern the resurrection. If our certainty about the Hour ever thins into something vague and distant, ayah 3 is where to go back to.

passages.title: Mocking the messenger, warned by sky and earth
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is about

These three ayat capture a single exchange: those who disbelieve sneering at the Prophet ﷺ for teaching that the dead will be raised, and Allah's reply. Ayah 7 gives us their mockery in their own words, ayah 8 gives us the false choice they built out of it, and ayah 9 answers them — not with argument alone, but by turning their eyes to the sky above them and the earth beneath them, which are at once the proof of Allah's power and, should He will it, the instruments of His punishment. What holds the three together is one theme: **they thought resurrection was too far-fetched to take seriously, and Allah shows them that the evidence is all around them.**

## The mockery in ayah 7: "a man"

Ibn Kathir opens by saying that here Allah tells us how the disbelievers and heretics denied that the Hour would come, and mocked the Messenger ﷺ for speaking of it.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out how the mockery actually worked, and it is worth slowing down over. In an exercise of mockery they used to say to one another, in effect: *come, let us identify an unusual person for your benefit — someone who loves to tell you how, when you die and become dust, totally powdered into countless particles, even after all that, you will be brought into a new creation, all reshaped into the form you once were and made to stand up alive.*

Notice the phrase **"a man"** (رَجُلٍ, *rajul*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes a sharp observation: the person alluded to is obviously none other than the Holy Prophet ﷺ, who used to tell people that the Qiyāmah — the Day of Resurrection — would come, when the dead would become alive once again, and who exhorted people to put their faith in it. **All these people who were deriding him knew him perfectly well.** Yet in this context they mention him as though they knew nothing else about him at all — nothing except that he tells people the dead will rise on the Day of Qiyāmah. They had purposely elected to refer to him in that manner, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, just to mock and deride him.

This is a recognisable move. Reduce a person to the one claim of theirs you find easiest to ridicule, strip away everything that would make a listener take them seriously, and the ridicule does the work that argument could not. The Qur'an records their sentence as they said it, and in recording it, exposes it.

## The language: مُزِّقْتُمْ كُلَّ مُمَزَّقٍ

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the key word. **مُزِّقْتُمْ (*muzziqtum*)** is a derivation from **مَزْق (*mazq*)**, which means splitting apart and rending to pieces. And **كُلَّ مُمَزَّقٍ (*kulla mumazzaq*)** — "totally torn" — means the disintegration of the human body in such a manner that all its particles get dispersed separately.

Ibn Kathir glosses it the same way: when your bodies have disintegrated into the earth and dispersed without a trace. So the picture is not merely of a corpse in a grave. It is of total dispersal — nothing left in one place, nothing recognisable, nothing to work from. The mockers chose the most extreme wording available to them, because the more absolute the scattering, the more absurd the reassembly was supposed to sound. Their rhetoric was doing the arguing.

And then, says Ibn Kathir, **إِنَّكُمْ** — "then you", meaning after all *that* has happened — **لَفِي خَلْقٍ جَدِيدٍ**, "will be created again anew": you will be restored to life and will receive provision anew.

## Ayah 8: a false choice with only two doors

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the drive of their remark in ayah 8. To them, the idea that all the totally disintegrated particles of the body would stand reassembled together, turn into the human body once again, and be alive as well, was so unreasonable to start with that there remained practically no question of entertaining or accepting it. Therefore, they reasoned, this claim of the Holy Prophet ﷺ must be one of two things: **either a deliberate attempt to fabricate a lie against Allah, or the words of an insane man**, no premise of whose statement is correct.

Ibn Kathir puts their reasoning in their own voice: by telling us this, he is doing one of two things — either he is deliberately fabricating something and saying that Allah has revealed it to him, or he is not doing it deliberately, but is deluded as crazy and insane people are. Hence: **أَفْتَرَىٰ عَلَى اللَّهِ كَذِبًا أَمْ بِهِ جِنَّةٌ** — "Has he invented a lie against Allah, or is there a madness in him?"

Their dilemma is airtight only if you have already decided the claim is impossible. That single unexamined assumption — *resurrection cannot happen* — is doing all the work, and ayah 9 will go straight at it.

## The reply: بَلْ — "Nay, rather…"

Allah answers, refuting their words, with a single overturning particle, **بَلْ (*bal*)**, "nay, rather": **بَلِ الَّذِينَ لَا يُؤْمِنُونَ بِالْآخِرَةِ فِي الْعَذَابِ وَالضَّلَالِ الْبَعِيدِ** — "Nay, but those who disbelieve in the Hereafter are themselves in a torment, and in far error."

Ibn Kathir's comment is worth reading twice: the matter is not as they claim or as they think. On the contrary, **Muhammad ﷺ is the one who is telling the truth, and is righteous and wise; he is the one who has brought the truth — and they are the foolish and ignorant liars.**

Notice where the charge lands. They had accused him of inventing a lie; Ibn Kathir's gloss places the word *liar* on them instead. And of **الضَّلَال الْبَعِيد**, "far error", Ibn Kathir says simply: **far from the truth in this world.**

And the torment: **فِي الْعَذَابِ** — Ibn Kathir explains this as their disbelief, which will lead them to the torment of Allah. There is something searching in that. The verse does not say they *will be* in torment; it says they **are** in it — because the kufr they are living in now is precisely the thing that carries them there. It is not a harmless present state awaiting a future verdict.

## Ayah 9: the evidence is on every side of them

**أَفَلَمْ يَرَوْا إِلَىٰ مَا بَيْنَ أَيْدِيهِمْ وَمَا خَلْفَهُمْ مِنَ السَّمَاءِ وَالْأَرْضِ** — "See they not what is before them and what is behind them, of the heaven and the earth?"

Then, says Ibn Kathir, Allah warns them of His power in the creation of the heavens and the earth. His gloss makes the image concrete: **wherever they go, in whatever direction, the heavens are above them and the earth is beneath them.** There is nowhere to stand that is outside the reach of this evidence. They needed only to look up, or down, or ahead, or behind.

He notes that this is like Allah's words: *"With Hands did We construct the heaven. Verily, We are Able to extend the vastness of space thereof. And We have spread out the earth; how Excellent Spreader thereof are We!"* (51:47–48).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān says this final verse carries **two chastening messages**, and they are two sides of one coin.

**First, an invitation to reason.** It proves that one can come to believe in the coming of Qiyāmah by pondering over what has been created in the heavens and the earth; and once the perfect power of Allah becomes visible through observation, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the element of *improbability* which prohibited its deniers from accepting it can stand removed. That is the precise point of contact with ayah 8: they said "unreasonable", and the answer given is not first a scolding but an instruction to *look* — because a sense of improbability is a judgement about power, and their estimate of Allah's power was simply too small.

Ibn Kathir spells out the inference. In looking at the creation of the heavens and the earth there is a sign of Allah's ability to recreate bodies and bring about the Resurrection, **because the One Who was able to create these heavens — with their vast reaches of space — and this earth, as deep and vast as it is, is able to recreate bodies and revive decayed bones.** He gathers other verses that make the same argument: *"Is not He Who created the heavens and the earth, Able to create the like of them? Yes, indeed!"* (36:81), and *"The creation of the heavens and the earth is indeed greater than the creation of mankind; yet most of mankind know not"* (40:57).

The scattering of a body over the earth felt to them like a problem too large for anyone to solve. Set beside the making of the heavens, it is the smaller task.

**Second, a warning.** Right along with this positive invitation to see and learn on their own, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, the deniers have also been served with a warning of punishment: should they continue to hold firmly to their attitude of rejection and denial, they should realise that it is within the power of Allah to make **these very same blessings become a punishment for them** — the earth swallowing them, or the sky cracking apart and falling on them.

That is the force of **إِنْ نَشَأْ نَخْسِفْ بِهِمُ الْأَرْضَ أَوْ نُسْقِطْ عَلَيْهِمْ كِسَفًا مِنَ السَّمَاءِ** — "If We will, We shall sink the earth with them, or cause a piece of the heaven to fall upon them." The same two things — sky and earth — that were just offered as evidence are now named as instruments. The floor you walk on and the roof over your head are not neutral facts; they are held for you.

Ibn Kathir then gives the sentence that keeps this from being mere menace. The meaning, he says, is: *if We wished, We could do that to them because of their wrongdoing and Our power over them* — **but We delay it because We are Patient and Forgiving.**

So the delay is not absence of notice, and not absence of power. Ibn Kathir names it for what it is: patience and forgiveness holding back what wrongdoing had earned.

## Who actually benefits: العَبْد المُنِيب

**إِنَّ فِي ذَٰلِكَ لَآيَةً لِكُلِّ عَبْدٍ مُنِيبٍ** — "Verily, in this is a sign for every *munīb* servant."

Ibn Kathir preserves two reports from the same early authority, Qatādah, transmitted through two different narrators:

- **Maʿmar, narrating from Qatādah:** *al-munīb* means every one who repents.
- **Sufyān, narrating from Qatādah:** *al-munīb* is the one who turns to Allah.

The two glosses sit easily together — turning back, and turning toward. And Ibn Kathir's own summary joins them to a third quality: in looking at the creation of the heavens and the earth there is a sign for every servant **who is intelligent and wise and who turns towards Allah.**

This is the quiet sting in the verse's ending, and it explains why the same sky produces belief in one person and nothing at all in another. The evidence is public — it is over every head. But it discloses itself as a *sign* to the one who is inclined to turn. The mockers of ayah 7 had the same heaven above them and the same earth beneath them, and drew nothing from either.

## Living it

**Ridicule is not an argument.** What the deniers brought against resurrection was not a refutation; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān shows it was a way of speaking — referring to the Prophet ﷺ as though he were nothing but "a man who tells you the dead will rise", purposely, in order to deride him. Ayah 8 shows their whole case resting on one unexamined premise. When something you know from revelation is made to sound laughable, check whether what you are being offered is evidence or only a sneer.

**Recalibrate your sense of what Allah can do.** Their error was arithmetic about power. Ibn Kathir's argument is available to anyone: look at the vast reaches of the heavens and the depth and breadth of the earth, and then ask honestly whether reassembling one body is the hard part.

**Read the delay correctly.** The most sobering line in this passage may be Ibn Kathir's *"but We delay it because We are Patient and Forgiving."* The sky staying where it is today says nothing about whether anything is wrong; it says something about forbearance. That is a door standing open, not a verdict already returned.

**Be *munīb*.** The sign is there for the one who turns — repenting, and turning toward Allah. Two people can look at the same night sky. What separates them is not eyesight.

passages.title: David and Solomon: gifts met with gratitude
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** Allah hands two prophet-kings, a father and his son, powers no one else has held: mountains that chant with Dawud, iron that softens in his hands, wind that carries Sulayman's throne, jinn that labour on his building sites. Yet the centre of gravity is not the power. It is the command dropped into the middle of it in ayah 13 — **"Work, O family of Dawud, in thankfulness"** — followed at once by *"and few of My servants are grateful."* Ayah 14 closes the circle: the man for whom the wind ran errands dies leaning on a stick, and a worm brings his kingdom's secret to light. Gift, gratitude, mortality — that is the arc.

## Why these stories appear *here*

Maʿārif ul Qurʾān supplies the link that unlocks the passage. The verses just before were answering people who denied life after death, who thought it plainly irrational that a body decomposed into dust could be revived. Allah's reply is not an argument but a memory: look at what He has already done that human reason would have ruled out — **iron soft as wax, copper flowing like water, wind harnessed as transport, mountains answering a human voice.** These are not decorative history lessons; they are exhibits in the case for the Resurrection.

## Dawud: the voice the mountains answered (ayah 10)

*"And indeed We bestowed grace (**faḍl**) on Dawud from Us."* Maʿārif explains **faḍl** as excess, favour, grace — something given *over and above* what others receive. Every prophet was granted some distinctive excellence; Dawud's included prophethood *and* kingship together. Ibn Kathir adds huge numbers of troops, and the ability to speak all languages.

But the gift the ayah names first is his voice. Ibn Kathir: Allah blessed him with a mighty voice, such that when he glorified Allah the firm, solid, high mountains joined in, and the free-roaming birds who leave in the morning and return in the evening stopped for him.

**The word أَوِّبِي (awwibī).** Ibn Kathir reports from Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid and others that it means *glorify Allah*. The root sense of **taʾwīb** is *to repeat or respond* — so the mountains and birds were commanded to **repeat after him**.

Maʿārif adds two points. Every created thing already glorifies Allah — *"there is not a single thing that does not extol His purity and praise, but you do not understand their extolling"* (17:44); what happened with Dawud was a **miracle**, so ordinary listeners must have heard and understood it, or nothing miraculous would have occurred. And it was no echo: reverberation in a dome or a well is mere physics, works for believer and disbeliever alike, and reflects nobody's excellence — whereas this is a grace bestowed on Dawud specifically.

**From the Sunnah.** Ibn Kathir records — citing it as "in the Ṣaḥīḥ" — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ heard Abū Mūsā al-Ashʿarī (may Allah be pleased with him) reciting at night, stopped, listened, and said that this man had been given one of the sweet melodious voices of the family of Dawud. Abū ʿUthmān an-Nahdī said he never heard any instrument more beautiful than Abū Mūsā's voice. A beautiful voice in reciting Allah's words is no vanity.

## Iron like thread, armour made to measure (ayat 10–11)

*"And We made the iron soft for him."* Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī, Qatādah, al-Aʿmash and others said he needed no fire and no hammer — **he could simply twist it in his hands like a thread**. Maʿārif: soft as wax, no tools needed.

Then the instruction: *"Make full-length coats of mail (**sābighāt**), and measure well in the **sard**."* *Sābighāt* is chain mail (Ibn Kathir), and Qatādah says Dawud was the first ever to make it, earlier peoples having worn plated armour. On **sard**, Ibn ʿAbbās (via ʿAlī bin Abī Ṭalḥah) said it means *a ring of iron*; Maʿārif adds that the word literally means *to weave*, while **qaddir** comes from **taqdīr**, making to a set measure. Mujāhid's gloss is the most vivid: *"Do not make the rivets too loose, so the rings shake, nor too tight, so they cannot move at all — but make it just right."*

Two things Maʿārif draws from that one word *qaddir*. First, **beauty in what we make is desirable**: the rings were to come out even and proportionate so the armour was strong *and* good to look at — and since Allah Himself gave the instruction, care over how man-made things look is something He approves. Second, some early commentators (citing *Rūḥ ul-Maʿānī*) read *taqdīr* as a fixed allotment of **time** for the craft, so that one pursuit does not swallow the day at the cost of worship and public duty.

Maʿārif notes that Allah took it upon Himself to teach His greatest prophets crafts — Dawud armour, Nūḥ the ark: *"Build the boat before Us"* (11:37), i.e. *as We tell you*. Hence its social point: no honest trade is low, and ranking people by occupation is a foreign import into Muslim life.

## Why Dawud, a king, needed a trade

Maʿārif reports this from the hadith authority Ḥāfiẓ Ibn ʿAsākir, as found in Tafsīr Ibn Kathīr.

At the height of his rule Dawud used to walk the markets **in disguise**, asking strangers what they thought of Dawud. Justice reigned, and whoever he asked praised him and gave thanks for the prevailing equity. Then Allah, for his education and grooming, sent an angel in the form of a man. Dawud put his usual question. The angel answered: *"Dawud is a very good man — better for himself and for his subjects than anyone. But he has one habit; without it he would be perfect."* Dawud asked what it was. The angel said: **"He takes his own and his family's expenses from the property of the Muslims — from the Bayt al-Māl."**

Dawud turned at once to Allah with self-reproach, praying: *teach me something I can do with my own hands, so I may support myself and my family from my own wages, and serve the Muslims and run their state without payment.* Allah answered — and the answer was the craft of making coats of mail. The honour befitting a prophet was that iron was made wax for him, so a short spell of work covered his needs and the rest of his time was free for worship and the business of state.

**The ruling Maʿārif draws.** A ruler whose whole time goes to state affairs *may* take his average living expenses from the Bayt al-Māl — likewise scholars who teach without pay, and the qāḍī (judge) and muftī in public service. But **if another livelihood is available that does not obstruct the service, that is better.** And from Dawud's canvassing of unguarded opinions Maʿārif draws a further note: *a person usually does not know his own shortcomings, so he must find them out from others* — Imam Mālik too attended to what ordinary people said of him.

## Sulayman: wind, molten copper, jinn (ayah 12)

*"And to Sulayman the wind: its morning course a month's journey, its evening course a month's journey."* Maʿārif: **ghuduww** is travel in the morning, **rawāḥ** travel in the evening — a month's distance from dawn to midday and another from evening to late night, two months in a single day. Ibn Kathir says the wind carried his carpet; Maʿārif, his throne, seating him with his courtiers. Al-Ḥasan al-Baṣrī gave the itinerary: setting out in the morning, the midday meal at Iṣṭakhr, the night at Kābul — each leg a month's ride for a swift rider.

*"And We caused a fount of **qiṭr** to flow for him."* Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, ʿIkrimah, Qatādah, as-Suddī and others: **qiṭr means copper**; the grammarian Khalīl said *molten* copper. Qatādah placed it in Yemen; Mujāhid's report has it running from Ṣanʿāʾ for three days' and nights' travel. Maʿārif: metal as hard as copper turned liquid, flowing like a stream — and **not hot** — so goods could be shaped from it easily.

*"And of the jinn, those who worked **before him**, by the leave of his Lord."* Ibn Kathir: by Allah's decree they built whatever he wanted and did other work besides. Maʿārif reads *before him* (**bayna yadayhi**) as deliberate — not the impersonal harnessing of sun and moon, but mastery over a workforce labouring in his presence like vassals. And *"whoever of them turned aside from Our command, We shall make him taste the punishment of the blazing Fire"*: Ibn Kathir, whoever tried to rebel and disobey. Most commentators, says Maʿārif, take this of Hellfire; others (via Qurṭubī) say that in this world too an angel was set over them who drove them with burning lashes when they slacked.

## What the jinn built (ayah 13)

*"They made for him whatever he wished — **maḥārīb**, **tamāthīl**, basins like water-tanks, and cauldrons fixed in place."*

**Maḥārīb**, plural of *miḥrāb*: Ibn Kathir, beautiful structures, the best and innermost part of a dwelling; Ibn Zayd, dwellings. Maʿārif traces the word to **ḥarb**, war — a man makes himself a seat of power and fights whoever encroaches on it; hence a palace's grandest chamber, and by extension mosques, are *maḥārīb*. **Jifān** (plural of *jafnah*) are great tubs holding water like the small cisterns called **jawāb**, and **qudūr rāsiyāt** cooking pots too huge to move, perhaps set on ovens of solid rock (aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk) — kitchen equipment on the scale of public works.

**Tamāthīl** — ʿAṭiyyah al-ʿAwfī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk and as-Suddī: *pictures*, of living and lifeless things alike (Maʿārif, citing Ibn al-ʿArabī). So images of the living were **not** forbidden in Sulayman's Sharīʿah, while in ours they are: earlier peoples slid from honouring images of revered figures to worshipping them, so Islam blocks the approaches to idolatry. From ʿAbdullāh ibn Masʿūd in Ṣaḥīḥ al-Bukhārī and Muslim: *"Of people, the most severely punished on the Day of Judgment will be the makers of images."*

## The hinge: "Work, O family of Dawud, in thankfulness"

Ibn Kathir: this means *work with thanks for the blessings We have bestowed on you in this world and the Hereafter* — and it shows that **thanks may be expressed by actions as much as by words and intentions**. Maʿārif notices the wording: the Qurʾān could have said the shorter *ushkurūnī*, "thank Me," but says *"work — in thankfulness."* The gratitude wanted from the House of Dawud was gratitude **in practice**.

Qurṭubī's definition, as Maʿārif gives it: to acknowledge that the blessing came from its giver, and then to use it in a way that pleases him and in obedience to him. The reverse follows — **using a gift against the wishes of the One who gave it is ingratitude, a practical denial of the gift.** Abū ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān al-Ḥubulī said: prayer is thanks, fasting is thanks, every good deed done for the sake of Allah is thanks, and the best of thanks is praise — recorded by Ibn Jarīr. (Maʿārif cites the same substance more briefly from a different early figure of the same kunya, Abū ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān as-Sulamī: prayer is gratitude, fasting is gratitude, every good deed is gratitude.) Muḥammad ibn Kaʿb al-Quraẓī: gratitude is another name for piety and righteous conduct.

And the family did it. Ibn Kathir reports the command was kept so faithfully by Dawud, Sulayman and their households, in word and deed, that **no hour passed in their homes without some member of the family standing in worship** — time was allotted to each, so Dawud's prayer-mat was never empty.

**From the Sunnah.** In the Two Ṣaḥīḥs, the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said the most beloved prayer to Allah is the prayer of Dawud — he slept half the night, stood a third of it, slept a sixth — and the most beloved fasting to Allah is the fasting of Dawud: he fasted a day and ate a day, *and he never fled the battlefield.* Note what closes that hadith: night devotion and daylight courage are cut from one cloth.

Reported by Tirmidhī and Abū Bakr al-Jaṣṣāṣ from ʿAṭāʾ ibn Yasār: when this ayah was revealed the Prophet ﷺ came to the pulpit, recited it, and said there are **three acts by which a person attains the same excellence granted to the House of Dawud**. Asked what they were, he said: *standing firm on justice whether pleased or displeased; taking the path of moderation in prosperity and in adversity; and fearing Allah both in private and in public.*

**Dawud's question.** Ibn Abī Ḥātim narrated from Fuḍayl that when the command to give thanks came, Dawud said: *"O Lord, how can I thank You, when thanks itself is a blessing from You?"* Allah said: *"Now you have truly thanked Me — for you have realised that it is a blessing from Me."* Gratitude begins where the illusion of self-sufficiency ends.

Then the verdict: *"and few of My servants are grateful."* Ibn Kathir calls it a statement of reality; Maʿārif, a spur to be among the few.

## The death that no one noticed (ayah 14)

*"Then when We decreed death for him, nothing informed them of his death except a creature of the earth eating away his staff; and when he fell, it became clear to the jinn that had they known the Unseen they would not have remained in the humiliating labour."*

**The word minsaʾah.** Maʿārif: a staff or pole of authority. Some early commentators held it a loan-word from Ethiopic; others derived it from *nasaʾa*, to drive away or push back — a stick being what you push harmful things away with, hence "the instrument of removal."

**What happened.** Ibn Kathir: Allah concealed Sulayman's death from the jinn subjugated to hard labour. He remained leaning on his staff — so Ibn ʿAbbās, Mujāhid, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah said — nearly a year; when a creature of the earth, a kind of worm, ate through the stick, it weakened and he fell, and only then was it apparent that he had died long before. Maʿārif fills in the account from Ibn ʿAbbās and other tafsīr authorities: Bayt al-Maqdis, begun by Dawud and completed by Sulayman, still had work outstanding, assigned to the jinn — refractory by nature, kept at it only by fear of him, certain to stop the moment they learned he had died. So, by Allah's leave, Sulayman entered the *miḥrāb*, made of clear glass so he could be seen from outside, and stood as he always did in worship, resting lightly on his staff, so that when his soul was taken his body would stay upright. The jinn dared not come close and peer at him; they worked on a full year, and when the work was done Allah empowered the termite.

**Why the Qurʾān tells us this.** Ibn Kathir is compact: it became clear to jinn and men alike that the jinn do *not* know the Unseen as they imagined and as they used to deceive people into believing — *"it became clear to the people that they were lying."* Maʿārif expands: the jinn cross great distances in moments and learn of events humans cannot, and when they relayed such news people took it for knowledge of the Unseen — the jinn may well have claimed as much themselves. This death exposed it: had they known the Unseen they would not have spent a year in *"the humiliating punishment"* — which here means the hard labour itself.

Maʿārif's lessons, plainly: **no one escapes death, and none meets it before its hour** — a king commanding wind, jinn and birds had no exemption. **When Allah wills a thing done, He arranges it as He wills** — even a dead man kept standing so a sanctuary could be finished. **Every cause works only as long as Allah permits**: the staff held until the termite was sent, then it simply failed — so with every prop we lean on. And **a door to false worship was shut**, since people dazzled by the jinn's feats might have venerated them. Hence Qurṭubī's two reasons for Sulayman's arrangement: that the remaining work be completed, and that people learn the jinn are ignorant and helpless.

**One last echo of the theme.** In a narration of ʿAbdullāh ibn ʿAmr reported by Imām an-Nasāʾī with sound chains, the Prophet ﷺ said that when Sulayman completed Bayt al-Maqdis he made supplications that were answered — among them that whoever enters that mosque intending nothing but prayer leave it purified of every sin, as pure as the day his mother bore him. And in the report of as-Suddī, standing on the Ṣakhrah, the first thing he asked of Allah — who had given him the power and resources to finish it — was **the ability to thank Him for it**; then to be taken while holding the faith Allah chose for him, and mercy, healing, safety and sufficiency for whoever entered.

## Living it

- **Treat the gift as a trust with a Giver.** *"Work righteousness"* in ayah 11 means, Ibn Kathir says, *with regard to the blessings Allah has given you* — sealed with *"Truly I am All-Seeing of what you do,"* which he explains as watching you, seeing all you do and say. We affirm that seeing as Allah described it, without likening it to ours and without emptying it of meaning.
- **Do the work well and to measure** — even the rivets; even the hours the workshop takes before worship and duty get their share.
- **Eat from your own hands where you can**, as a prophet-king asked to do rather than live off the public purse.
- **Let gratitude be a verb.** Prayer is thanks; fasting is thanks; justice when you are angry, moderation when you are rich, fear of Allah when nobody is watching — those three, the Prophet ﷺ said, earn what the House of Dawud was given. And when it dawns on you that even your thanking is His gift, you have begun to thank Him properly.

passages.title: Sheba's gardens lost through ingratitude
passages.tafsir:
These five ayat tell the story of one nation — Saba' (Sheba) in the Yemen — given about as good a life as this world offers, which lost every part of it by refusing to be thankful. The arc: the blessing (15), the turning away and the flood (16), the verdict (17), a second blessing also spurned (18), and their erasure, closing with the one kind of person who profits from the story (19).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes the flow: the earlier ayat warned those who denied prophethood and the Day of Judgment and failed to grasp how complete Allah's power is; then came the miracles of earlier prophets and the accounts of Dawud and Sulayman (peace be upon them). Saba' follows as the case study.

## Who Saba' were

Ibn Kathir explains that Saba' refers to the kings and people of the Yemen. The Tubba' kings (At-Tababa'ah) were of them, and Bilqis — the queen who met Sulayman, peace be upon him — was one of them. They lived, he says, "a life of enviable luxury," with abundant provision, crops and fruit. Allah sent them messengers telling them to eat of His provision and thank Him by worshipping Him alone; they held to that as long as Allah willed, and then turned away.

Ibn Jarir recorded from Farwah bin Musayk Al-Ghutayfi (may Allah be pleased with him) that a man asked, "O Messenger of Allah, tell me about Saba' — was it a land or a woman?" He ﷺ replied that it was neither a land nor a woman, but a man who had ten children, six of whom went south to the Yemen and four north to Ash-Sham, and he named the tribes descended from each. Ibn Kathir notes At-Tirmidhi recorded it more fully in his Jami' and graded it *hasan gharib*; Maʿārif reports the same substance from Imam Ahmad, from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him). Ibn Kathir clarifies that "ten children" means ten lines of descent, not sons of his own loins, and that the six-south-four-north detail describes what happened *after* the flood. The genealogists, including Muhammad bin Ishaq, say his name was ʿAbd Shams bin Yashjub bin Yaʿrub bin Qahtan, and that he was called *Saba'* because his was the first Arab tribe to disperse — the very reason for the name is the fate ayah 19 announces.

Ibn Kathir, citing Sahih Al-Bukhari, notes that the Prophet ﷺ passed men of Aslam practising archery and said, "Shoot, O sons of Ismaʿil, for your father was an archer" — and Aslam was a tribe of the Ansar, who descended from Ghassan, from the Arabs of Yemen from Saba', settling in Yathrib when Saba' was scattered by the flood. The people of Madinah were the far end of this very story.

**When did it happen?** Maʿārif, quoting al-Qurtubi from Qushairi, places Saba' after ʿIsa (peace be upon him) and before the Prophet ﷺ — in the period called *fatrah*, the gap. Maʿārif also reports (from Muhammad Ibn Ishaq, via Ibn Kathir) that Allah sent thirteen prophets to warn them, which raises a problem, since the majority hold no prophet was sent during the fatrah. The answer Maʿārif gives from Ruh ul-Maʿani: the prophets may have come earlier, the people's defiance hardening during the fatrah, so that the punishment fell in that period.

## Ayah 15: what exactly was the "sign"?

"Indeed there was for Saba' a sign in their dwelling place" — **two gardens on the right and on the left.** Ibn Kathir explains this as the two sides where the mountains stood, with the people's land in between.

Water came down from between two mountains, swollen by rainfall and the valleys, and their ancient kings built a huge, strong dam that held it at a high level between the peaks. Then they planted, and harvested the finest fruit imaginable. This was the dam of Maʿarib — Ibn Kathir places it three days' journey from Sanʿa'; Maʿārif, reporting from him, gives three miles. Maʿārif adds, on the authority of Mazhari, that it had three gates at appropriate levels so the reservoir could be drawn down in order until the next rains refilled it, and a tank beneath with twelve outlets feeding twelve canals. Maʿārif adds that the slopes to right and left of the city were landscaped with rows of gardens fed by those canals.

**Why "two gardens" for many?** Maʿārif notes that the gardens were many, but the Qur'an says *jannatān* because all those in the row on one slope count as one garden and all on the other as the second.

Qatadah and a number of the Salaf said a woman could walk beneath the trees with a basket on her head and the fruit would fall and fill it without her lifting a hand. Others said the land had no flies, mosquitoes, fleas or vermin at all — the climate was temperate and the people healthy; and Maʿārif reports from Ibn Kathir that when travellers arrived with parasites in their clothes, these simply died off. Ibn Kathir notes the purpose: Allah took care of them so that they would single Him out and worship Him alone.

**"Eat of the provision of your Lord, and be grateful to Him."** This was said to them, Maʿārif explains, through His prophets: use the ample means Allah has provided, and remain grateful through good deeds and unfailing obedience. Ibn Kathir defines gratitude as giving thanks "by worshipping Him alone."

**"A fair land and an Oft-Forgiving Lord."** Ibn Kathir reads *Oft-Forgiving* as the offer standing behind the blessing — "He would forgive you if you continue to worship Him alone." Maʿārif draws it further: by joining a good city to a Most-Forgiving Lord the mention of blessing is made complete. This good life need not be confined to the present world; had they stayed grateful, the greater and lasting blessings of the Hereafter were promised too — and the naming of *Ghafūr* covers human slipping as well: should they inadvertently fail in gratitude or fall short through negligence, He is a great Forgiver.

## Ayah 16: the turning away, and the dam

**"But they turned away."** From what? Ibn Kathir: from worshipping Allah alone and from thanking Him for what He had given — and they began worshipping the sun instead of Allah. He cites the hoopoe's report to Sulayman: "I found her and her people worshipping the sun instead of Allah, and Shaytan has made their deeds fair seeming to them, and has barred them from the way, so they have no guidance" (27:24).

**"So We sent against them the flood of the ʿarim."** Maʿārif notes that *ʿarim* carries several recognised meanings, but the meaning most in keeping with the Qur'anic context — given in lexicons such as the *Qāmūs* and Jawhari's *Sihāh*, and reported from Ibn ʿAbbas (may Allah be pleased with him) by al-Qurtubi — is a dam built to block water. So the phrase is, literally, *the flood of the dam*, and Maʿārif points out the irony: the very ʿarim that had been their security and prosperity was turned by Allah into the instrument of their ruin.

**How it fell.** Ibn Kathir reports from a group of early authorities — Ibn ʿAbbas, Wahb bin Munabbih, Qatadah and Ad-Dahhak — that when Allah willed to punish them He sent creatures of the earth against the dam: large rats, which holed it. Wahb bin Munabbih said they had found it written in their scriptures that the dam would be destroyed by these rats, so for a time they brought cats to guard it — "but when the decree came to pass, the rats overran the cats and went into the dam, making a hole in it, and it collapsed." Qatadah and others said the rat is the desert rat: they gnawed at the base until it weakened, then the flood season came, the water struck the weakened structure and it gave way, tearing down the valley and destroying everything in its path — buildings, trees, all of it.

Maʿārif adds that some far-sighted people, seeing the rats, made arrangements and left the area one by one; others stayed, and shifted only once the flood came, while many were swallowed by it.

**What replaced the gardens.** With the canals dry, the trees on the slopes withered, and the two gardens were exchanged for two of a completely different kind. *Ukul khamṭ* — bitter, bad fruit — was explained by Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, ʿIkrimah, ʿAṭa' Al-Khurasani, Qatadah and As-Suddi as the *arāk* and bitter fruit; Maʿārif describes the arāk as a pungent, thorny desert tree, and notes Jawhari's remark that one kind of arāk does bear edible fruit, though what grew here was bad in taste. Abu ʿUbaidah said any thorny tree of bitter taste is called *khamṭ*. *Athl*: Al-ʿAwfi and Ibn ʿAbbas said it means tamarisk — the majority view per Maʿārif — whose fruit is not worth eating; others said a tree resembling tamarisk, or the gum acacia or mimosa, "and Allah knows best." *Sidr*, the lote, comes in two kinds, Maʿārif explains — cultivated, sweet and lightly thorned, or wild, mostly thorns with little bitter fruit — and *qalīl*, "few," perhaps signals the wild kind. Ibn Kathir reads the "few" differently: because the lote was the best of the trees they were left with, there was only a little of it.

Ibn Kathir sums up: the exchange came because of their disbelief, their associating others with Allah, and their denying the truth and turning to falsehood.

## Ayah 17: the verdict, and who this punishment is for

"This is how We requited them for their kufr. And do We requite in this way any but the ungrateful?"

Maʿārif: *kufr* means both ingratitude and denial of the true faith, and here both senses apply, because they did both — they were ungrateful for the blessings and they rejected the thirteen prophets sent to them. The word closing the ayah, *kafūr*, Maʿārif identifies as an emphatic form of *kāfir*: one who is very ungrateful, or an absolute disbeliever.

Taken absolutely, "We do not punish any but the *kafūr*" would clash with the many ayat and sound ahadith establishing that sinning Muslims are punished too, in the measure of their deeds — though they are finally brought out of the Fire because of their faith and admitted into Paradise. The resolution given from Ruh ul-Maʿani is that the ayah speaks not of punishment absolutely but of *mass* punishment of the kind sent on Saba', which is particular to disbelievers and does not befall Muslim sinners. Ibn Kathir's citations agree: Mujahid said, "He does not punish anyone except the disbelievers," and Al-Hasan Al-Basri said, "Allah the Almighty has spoken the truth: no one will be punished in a manner that befits the sin except the ungrateful disbelievers" — because a believer, being no *kafūr*, receives some concession regarding his sins.

Maʿārif then quotes a saying of the Tabiʿi Ibn Khiyarah, which it sources to Ibn Kathir: the punishment of sin is that the sinner becomes sluggish in acts of worship, his economic condition becomes straitened, and enjoyment itself becomes hard to bear — Ibn Khiyarah explaining that last part by saying that when one is blessed with something lawful to enjoy, some reason comes along to spoil the enjoyment. This, Maʿārif comments, is the punishment given to Muslim sinners; no open punishment hits them from the heavens or from beneath the earth. Maʿārif relays one further reading from Ruh ul-Maʿani, citing *Kashf*: punishment *as* punishment is given only to the disbeliever, and whatever pain a believing sinner suffers through fire is an apparent punishment whose real purpose is to cleanse him, like gold heated in a furnace to remove its unwanted sediment.

## Ayah 18: the second blessing — the road

Ibn Kathir describes the ease of their travel: they needed to carry neither provisions nor water, because wherever they stopped they found water and fruit — they could take their noontime rest in one town and stay overnight in the next. "The towns which We had blessed" are, according to Mujahid, Al-Hasan, Saʿid bin Jubayr, Qatadah, Ad-Dahhak, As-Suddi, Ibn Zayd and others, the towns of Syria; the caravans ran from the Yemen to Syria through towns easy to be seen and connected to one another. Al-ʿAwfi reported from Ibn ʿAbbas: "the towns which We had blessed by putting Jerusalem among them." Maʿārif likewise takes the rural areas of Syria to be meant, noting that the Qur'an's references to the descent of mercy are specifically related to that land, and it counts three distinct favours in this one ayah:

1. **The chain of towns** — *qurā ẓāhirah*, "towns easy to be seen": clear and visible, known to travellers (Ibn Kathir). Maʿārif notes that the distance from Maʿarib to Syria was long and the routes uneven by the standards of that world, so Allah placed a series of towns at intermittent distances the whole way.
2. **The measured stages** — "and We measured the journey between them," which Ibn Kathir explains as an arrangement meeting the travellers' needs, and Maʿārif as habitations set close by the main road at balanced, equal intervals, so a traveller could rest and eat at one town, set off after Zuhr, and reach the next by sundown.
3. **Safety** — "Travel in them by night and day, secure." Theft and highway robbery were unknown; one could travel at any hour without hesitation or concern.

## Ayah 19: the prayer no one should ever make

"But they said: 'Our Lord! Make the stages of our journey longer' — and they wronged themselves."

Ibn ʿAbbas, Mujahid, Al-Hasan and others explained it, as Ibn Kathir reports: they wanted to travel long distances through empty wilderness, where they would have to carry provisions, cross intense heat, and travel in a state of fear. Maʿārif compares them to the Children of Israel, who received *mann* and *salwā* free of cost, grew bored of it, and asked for vegetables and greens instead. Nothing was taken from Allah; the injury of ingratitude lands on the ungrateful.

**"So We made them tales, and We tore them utterly to pieces."** Ibn Kathir explains *aḥādīth*: they became something for people to talk about when they converse in the evening — how Allah's plan overtook them and dispersed them after their united life of luxury. And *mazzaqnāhum*, Maʿārif notes, is from *tamzīq*, to tear and scatter a people, or to destroy a kingdom: some of the inhabitants of Maʿarib were destroyed on the spot, others scattered in small groups across various countries. Their scattering became proverbial in Arabia — the Arabs say of a people who have broken up, "They have been scattered like Saba'," in all directions.

Maʿārif relays from Ibn Kathir and other commentators that a soothsayer came to know of the flood shortly before it struck, sold his entire property, and then told his people to leave, directing them to different destinations: the tribe of Azd went to ʿAmman, Ghassan to Busra in Syria, and Aws and Khazraj towards Yathrib, the home of date palms. These, says Ibn Kathir, are the people meant by "We tore them utterly to pieces."

## The closing line: who this story is for

"Indeed, in that are signs for every steadfast, grateful one" — *li-kulli ṣabbārin shakūr*. Maʿārif renders the phrase "everyone who is ever-patient, fully grateful": when distress or pain comes he holds patience over it, and when comfort comes he is readily grateful for it. That, Maʿārif observes, is a way of living in which a person always comes out ahead, whatever his circumstances.

Ibn Kathir explains why these two qualities: in the punishment these people suffered, and in the way their blessings and good health were turned into retribution for their disbelief and sins, there is a lesson and an indication for whoever is steadfast in the face of adversity and grateful for blessings. Saba' had ease and were not grateful; then they were given hardship, and there was nothing in them to bear it with.

Hence the hadith Ibn Kathir brings from Saʿd bin Abi Waqqas (may Allah be pleased with him), recorded by Imam Ahmad and also, Ibn Kathir notes, by An-Nasa'i in *Al-Yawm wal-Laylah*, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: "I am amazed at what Allah has decreed for the believer; if something good befalls him, he praises his Lord and gives thanks, and if something bad befalls him, he praises his Lord and has patience. The believer will be rewarded for everything, even the morsel of food which he lifts to his wife's mouth." Ibn Kathir notes there is a corroborating report in the Two Sahihs from Abu Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him): "How amazing is the affair of the believer! Allah does not decree anything for him but it is good for him. If something good happens to him, he gives thanks, and that is good for him; if something bad happens to him, he bears it with patience, and that is good for him. This is not for anyone except the believer." Maʿārif cites this same hadith from the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim. Ibn Kathir also relays that Mutarrif used to say: "How blessed is the grateful, patient servant. If he is given something, he gives thanks, and if he is tested, he bears it with patience."

**Living it.** Saba' fell not through some spectacular crime but by a slow slide: enjoying the gift, forgetting the Giver, then finding the gift itself tiresome. The warning is aimed at whoever is currently comfortable — so the response to a blessing is to spend it in obedience and name its source. Maʿārif notes that some commentators take *ṣabbār* in the general sense of patience, which includes remaining firm in every act of obedience as well as abstaining from sins, so that such a believer is comprehensively attuned to patience and gratitude in all conditions — and for him every act of patience is gratitude and every act of gratitude is patience. Allah knows best.

passages.title: Satan's guess came true, though he held no power
passages.tafsir:
These two ayat step back from the ruined gardens of Saba' and name the force at work behind such a collapse: Iblis had a thought — an assumption — about human beings, and with most of them it proved true, yet he was never given any authority over them. Ayah 20 states the outcome (they followed him, all except a group of true believers); ayah 21 removes the excuse (he had no authority — and, as Ibn 'Abbas explained it, no proof) and states the purpose (to distinguish the one who believes in the Hereafter from the one who is in doubt about it), closing with the reassurance that your Lord is Watchful over everything.

## Why this comes right after Saba'

Ibn Kathir makes the join explicit. Having described Saba' — a people who "followed their desires, and the Shaytan" — Allah now turns to their counterparts in every age: "those who follow Iblis and their own desires, and who go against wisdom and true guidance."

So the passage is not a change of subject. It is the diagnosis after the case study. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, commenting on ayah 19, describes just how far the ingratitude of Saba' went: the blessing Allah had placed there was designed to eliminate the hardships of travel, and they dismissed it — praying instead that their Lord make the distances of their journeys longer, so that the settlements would not appear at such close intervals, wishing to see hard stretches of forest or wilderness that would demand some rough traversing. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān compares their case to that of Banu Isra'il, who received the excellent sustenance of *mann* and *salwa* free of cost, grew bored of it, and asked Allah to replace it with vegetables and greens. In return for that ingratitude came the punishment already mentioned — the flood of the dam — and its ultimate consequence is stated in ayah 19 itself: they were virtually expunged from this world, leaving nothing behind but idle tales of their wealth and luxury.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that the word مَزَّقْنَاهُمْ (*mazzaqnāhum*) derives from *tamzīq*, which means to tear and scatter a people, or to destroy a kingdom: some of the inhabitants of the city of Ma'arib were destroyed on the spot, and others were scattered so that small groups of them spread out to various countries. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān relates from Ibn Kathir and other commentators the long narrative of a soothsayer who learned of the coming flood shortly before it struck, sold his property, and urged his people to leave — after which the tribe of Azd went towards 'Amman, the Ghassan to Busra in Syria, and the Aws, Khazraj and Banu 'Uthman set off towards Yathrib, the home of date palms. Their dispersal became proverbial in Arabia: on such occasions the Arabs would use the idiom تَفَرَّقُوا اَیَادِیَ — "these people got scattered away as were the luxury-laden people of the Saba'."

Hold that picture in mind, because ayah 20 tells you who was walking beside them the whole way down.

## Ayah 20: the thought that proved true

**وَلَقَدْ صَدَّقَ عَلَيْهِمْ إِبْلِيسُ ظَنَّهُ** — "And indeed Iblis did prove true his thought about them," or, as the translation renders it, "Iblis' assumption about them has come true."

Read the sentence carefully as it stands. What Iblis had was a ظَنّ (*zann*) — rendered here as a thought, an assumption — and what the ayah reports is that it *proved true*, and that it proved true through them: **فَاتَّبَعُوهُ** — "and they followed him." The one whose expectation was borne out is the enemy; the ones who bore it out were the people themselves.

**What exactly was that thought?** Here Ibn Kathir reports that Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) and others said this ayah is like the ayah in which Allah tells us how Iblis refused to prostrate to Adam, peace be upon him, and then said:

> "See this one whom You have honoured above me — if You give me respite to the Day of Resurrection, I will surely seize and mislead his offspring, all but a few!" (17:62)

and:

> "Then I will come to them from before them and behind them, from their right and from their left, and You will not find most of them as thankful ones." (7:17)

Ibn Kathir adds that there are many ayat which refer to this matter. So the "thought" of ayah 20 is that ancient boast, made in the moment of his refusal: *give me time and I will get almost all of them — and You will not find most of them thankful.*

**"Except a group" — إِلَّا فَرِيقًا.** Ibn Kathir's rendering names them: "all except a group of true believers." Even his own boast in 17:62 had to say "all but a few." The exception clause is small in words and enormous in meaning: to be part of *that* group is the whole aim of a believing life.

## Ayah 21: he had no authority — and no proof

**وَمَا كَانَ لَهُ عَلَيْهِمْ مِنْ سُلْطَانٍ** — "And he had no authority over them."

If ayah 20 could tempt anyone into fatalism — *the devil got us, what could we do* — ayah 21 shuts that door immediately. Whatever happened, it did not happen because Iblis held authority over them.

Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) gives a precise gloss on *sulṭān* here: **"This means, he had no proof."** That is a striking reading. Where the translations render *sulṭān* as "authority," Ibn 'Abbas reads it in the sense of a proof — evidence, an argument. On that reading, ayah 21 is a verdict of full human responsibility: those who followed him were not compelled by any proof he held. They were, in Ibn Kathir's words at the opening of the passage, people who "follow Iblis and their own desires, and who go against wisdom and true guidance."

**The stated purpose: إِلَّا لِنَعْلَمَ.** Ibn Kathir explains the clause "except that We might test him who believes in the Hereafter, from him who is in doubt about it" as meaning: "We gave him power over them only to show who believes in the Hereafter and that it will come to pass."

So whatever power Iblis has over people is not something he seized; it was given, and given for a stated purpose — in Ibn Kathir's own words, *to show*, and *to distinguish* "these believers from those who are in doubt about the Hereafter." And Ibn Kathir spells out what that belief actually consists of: that the Hereafter will come to pass, that people will be brought to account and rewarded or punished accordingly, "so that he will worship his Lord properly in this world." Belief in the Hereafter, in this reading, is not an item of information stored in the mind; it is the conviction that shapes how a person worships today.

**وَرَبُّكَ عَلَىٰ كُلِّ شَيْءٍ حَفِيظٌ** — "And your Lord is Watchful over everything."

The passage ends on a divine attribute, and Ibn Kathir reads it in two directions at once: it means "despite His watching, those who follow Iblis go astray, but by His watching and care, the believers who follow the Messengers are saved."

That is, the same watchfulness is over every single thing. For the one who follows Iblis, going astray happens in full view of Allah. For the believer who follows the Messengers, that very same watching is care, and it is by it that he is saved. In a passage about a nation destroyed and an enemy's assumption borne out, the last word is your Lord's watching and care.

## Living it

**Deny his assumption its confirmation.** The ayah says his thought proved true *and they followed him*. It was their following that bore it out. Every choice of obedience over desire is a place where that does not happen. Aim to be part of the "group of true believers" the ayah excepts.

**Ask what proof there is.** Ibn 'Abbas' gloss is a practical weapon: he had no proof. And Ibn Kathir describes those who fall as following "Iblis and their own desires," going "against wisdom and true guidance." So when something pulls you, ask which of the two it is — an argument from wisdom and guidance, or a desire dressed up as one.

**Treat the pull itself as the exam.** Ibn Kathir says the power granted was granted "only to show who believes in the Hereafter," to distinguish the believer from the one in doubt. So the moment of temptation is not an interruption of your religious life — it is the question paper. And Ibn Kathir ties belief in the Hereafter directly to conduct: knowing that people will be brought to account, a person "will worship his Lord properly in this world."

**Guard gratitude.** Iblis' own words include the claim, "You will not find most of them as thankful ones" (7:17). Which is why Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's treatment of the closing phrase of ayah 19 — "signs for everyone who is ever-patient, fully grateful" — is worth carrying into this passage: the person who observes patience when faced with distress or pain, and is readily grateful when blessed with comfort, lives "a life style in which one always comes out a winner," ending up with nothing but gains whatever his circumstances.
