Maʿārif ul Qurʼān quotes here a Hadith of Sayyidna Abu Hurairah (may Allah be pleased with him) appearing in the Sahih of al-Bukhari and Muslim, in which the Holy Prophet ﷺ is reported to have said that unique is the state of life a true believer is always in: whatever Allah decrees for him turns for him into nothing but good and profitable — if he is blessed or has the desire of his heart fulfilled, he thanks Allah and it becomes good and beneficial for him in the Hereafter; and if he suffers pain or distress, he bears it with considered patience for which he is rewarded in a big way, so that the suffering too becomes good and beneficial for him. (Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites it from Ibn Kathir.)

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that some commentators take صَبَّار (*ṣabbār*, "very patient") in the general sense of *ṣabr* — which includes remaining firm in all acts requiring obedience as well as abstaining from sins. On that explanation, a true believer remains comprehensively attuned to *ṣabr* and *shukr* under all conditions, so that "every sabr is shukr and every shukr is sabr." And Allah knows best.

passages.title: Powerless gods, and a Lord who will judge between us
passages.tafsir:
This passage is a courtroom cross-examination of idolatry, dictated to the Prophet ﷺ line by line. The command comes: **"Say."** — in ayah 22, twice in ayah 24, and then in each of 25, 26 and 27. Ayah 22 strips the false gods of every conceivable claim to power; ayah 23 removes their last refuge, the hope that they might at least put in a good word; ayah 24 turns to the one thing the idolators already admitted; and ayat 25–27 close the case by separating the two parties and handing the verdict to Allah. The Prophet ﷺ is not asked to shout down his opponents — he is handed arguments, and a way of putting them that leaves his opponents room to think.

## Ayah 22: three beliefs, taken apart in one sentence

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān observes: these ayat are aimed at **three different kinds of idol-worshipper**, and each clause answers one of them.

**First** were those who held that idols made of stone were partners of Allah and His associates in all His powers. The opening of ayah 22 answers them: *they possess not even the weight of a speck of dust, either in the heavens or on the earth.* The measure named is **mithqāl dharratin** — as Maʿārif ul Qurʼān renders it, not even "to the measure of a particle." Not "little power": no power at all, nowhere in the universe. Ibn Kathir places beside it the ayah *And those, whom you invoke or call upon instead of Him, own not even a Qitmir* (35:13).

Then, *nor have they any share in either.* Ibn Kathir explains: they own nothing **independently, and nothing as partners** either. The first clause denies sole ownership; this one denies even a shareholding.

**Second** were those who believed the idols were Allah's helpers in managing the affairs of the universe — junior officials in a vast administration. The end of ayah 22 answers them: *nor is there for Him any supporter from among them.* Ibn Kathir: Allah has no rival among these whose support He seeks in any matter — "on the contrary, all of creation is in need of Him and is enslaved by Him." This is the thesis Ibn Kathir sees stated here: Allah is the One and Only, the Self-Sufficient Master, with no peer or partner, independent in His command, with none who can share in it, dispute it, or overturn it.

**Third** — the subtlest group, and the one closest to how religion actually goes wrong — were people who did *not* claim the idols were gods or helpers of Allah at all. They maintained only that these figures were *so close* to Allah that their intercession was always approved by Him, so that whoever had the advantage of their intercession would have his desires fulfilled. That is answered in ayah 23.

## Ayah 23: intercession is not a private channel

*No intercession will be of any benefit with Him, except by those He permits.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the double refutation: the assumption that the idols are close to Allah is itself false — "they are neither close to Allah, nor do they have any power of intercession before Him."

But the ayah does more than refute stone idols: it sets out the rule of intercession as such. Ibn Kathir: because of Allah's might, majesty and pride, **no one would dare to intercede with Him in any matter** except after being granted permission to do so. He lines up the confirming ayat — *Who is he that can intercede with Him except with His permission?* (2:255); *And there are many angels in the heavens, whose intercession will avail nothing except after Allah has given leave for whom He wills and is pleased with* (53:26); *and they cannot intercede except for him with whom He is pleased. And they stand in awe for fear of Him* (21:28).

The ayah says something more exact than "intercession is denied": intercession is **real, and entirely dependent**. Ibn Kathir gives the greatest instance of it. It was reported in the Two Sahihs, through more than one chain of narration, that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ — "the leader of the sons of Adam and the greatest intercessor before Allah" — will go to stand in **al-Maqām al-Maḥmūd**, the praised position, to intercede for all of mankind when their Lord comes to pass judgement upon them. He ﷺ said:

> "Then I will prostrate to Allah, may He be exalted, and He will leave me (in that position) as long as Allah wills, and He will inspire me to speak words of praise which I cannot mention now. Then it will be said, 'O Muhammad, raise your head. Speak, you will be heard; ask, you will be given; intercede, your intercession will be accepted…'"

Even the greatest intercession in creation begins in **prostration**, waits as long as Allah wills, and proceeds only when permission is spoken. So the idolators' calculation — cultivate the intermediary, and the Owner must comply — collapses at its root.

## The trembling of the heavens

The rest of ayah 23 opens a window onto the unseen: *until, when fear is banished from their hearts, they say, "What did your Lord say?" They say, "The truth."*

The verb is **fuzziʿa ʿan qulūbihim** — as Ibn Kathir explains it, "when the fear leaves their hearts." Something has to be removed before they can even speak. Ibn Kathir reports the view of Ibn Masʿūd (may Allah be pleased with him), Masruq and others: this too refers to the great degree of Allah's might and power — when He speaks words of revelation, the inhabitants of the heavens hear what He says and tremble with fear of Allah so much that they swoon.

He then names a long line of early authorities on the phrase — Ibn ʿAbbās, Ibn ʿUmar, Abū ʿAbd ar-Raḥmān as-Sulamī, ash-Shaʿbī, Ibrāhīm an-Nakhaʿī, aḍ-Ḍaḥḥāk, al-Ḥasan and Qatādah — all reading it as "when the fear is lifted from their hearts." What follows is a relay: the angels carrying the Throne tell those next to them, and so on, until the news reaches the inhabitants of the lowest heaven. And *they say, "The truth"* — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, they report what He said, **without adding or taking away anything**.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws the argument to its point: even the angels, who really *are* close to Allah, cannot intercede for anyone without His permission — and even when they are permitted, it is not easy for them, because of the awe of Allah in their hearts. When a command reaches them they become overcome, and only once they return to their normal condition do they ask one another about it, to be sure of its correct nature. If that is the condition of the angels, what exactly did the idol-worshippers imagine their stones were doing?

Then the ayah closes: *And He is the Most High, the Most Great* — **al-ʿAlī al-Kabīr**. The heavens shake, and He is above all of it.

## From the Sunnah: what the fortune-teller actually heard

Commenting on *al-ʿAlī al-Kabīr*, Ibn Kathir cites what al-Bukhari recorded in his Sahih — in his own tafsir of this very ayah — from Abu Hurayrah, may Allah be pleased with him, that the Prophet of Allah ﷺ said:

> "When Allah decrees a matter in heaven, the angels beat their wings in submission to His Words, making a sound like a chain striking a smooth rock. When the fear is banished from their hearts, they say, 'What is it that your Lord has said?' They say the truth, and He is the Most High, the Most Great. Then the one who is listening out hears that, and those who are listening out are standing one above the other" — Sufyan, one of the narrators, demonstrated with his hand, holding it vertically with the fingers outspread — "So he hears what is said and passes it on to the one below him, and that one passes it to the one who is below him, and so on until it reaches the lips of the soothsayer or fortune-teller. Maybe a meteor will hit him before he can pass anything on, or maybe he will pass it on before he is hit. He tells a hundred lies alongside it, but it will be said, 'Did he not tell us that on such and such a day, such and such would happen?' So they believe him because of the one thing which was heard from heaven."

Ibn Kathir notes this was recorded by al-Bukhari and not by Muslim, and that Abu Dawud, at-Tirmidhi and Ibn Majah also recorded it.

Two things come out of this. First, the sound-image: **a chain struck against smooth rock** — the response to Allah's decree is not discussion but that ringing, submissive beating of wings. Second, an explanation of the soothsayers' occasional accuracy: one snatched word from above, buried in a hundred lies, and people credit the whole enterprise for the sake of the one hit. It is a warning about how little truth is needed to launder a great deal of falsehood.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds a second report: it appears in the Sahih of Muslim that Ibn ʿAbbās reports from one of the Companions that the Prophet ﷺ said that when Allah gives a command, the angels who hold the Divine Throne begin reciting tasbīḥ (glorifying Allah), and hearing them the angels of the next lower heaven follow suit, and so on down to the lowest heaven; then they ask the angels who are close to the Throne, "What did your Lord say?" and are told, and in the same way those of the lower heavens ask those above them, until that chain of question and answer extends down through the heavens (Mazhari).

## Ayah 24: the question that answers itself

*Ask them: Who provides for you from the heavens and the earth?* Then, without waiting: *Say: Allah.*

Ibn Kathir explains why the Prophet ﷺ supplies the answer himself. Allah is unique in His power of creation and His giving of provision, and He is unique in His divinity also. **They already conceded the first half.** They used to admit that no one in heaven or on earth except Allah gave them provision — by sending down water and causing crops to grow. So the reply is put into the questioner's mouth because there was no honest alternative: they should therefore also realise that there is no god worthy of worship besides Him. Anything else is an incoherence one holds only by not looking at it.

## The wisdom of "either we or you"

Then: *And verily, either we or you are rightly guided or in plain error.*

Ibn Kathir reads it as an exclusive choice: one of the two sides must be speaking falsehood and one must be telling the truth. There is no way both parties could be following true guidance, or could both be misguided — "and we have produced the proof of Tawḥīd which indicates that your Shirk must be false." Qatādah said the Companions of Muhammad ﷺ said this to the idolators: "By Allah, we and you cannot be following the same thing, only one of us can be truly guided." ʿIkrimah and Ziyād bin Abī Maryam said the meaning is: we are rightly guided and you are in plain error.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān then draws out a lesson on **the psychology of the addressee in debate**. This address, it notes, is beamed at polytheists and disbelievers, and in their case what was needed had already been done: that Allah is the Creator, the Master, and all-powerful in the absolute sense had been proved decisively and explicitly; that idols and everything else other than Allah are weak and helpless had been demonstrated clearly. The occasion then "demanded that Mushriks are told in clear terms that they were ignorant and astray in bypassing Allah and electing to worship idols and shaitans." And yet, note what the Qur'an does **not** do: the disbelieving adversaries addressed in this ayah are not called kāfirs, infidels, disbelievers, or the ones gone astray. Instead a change was introduced in the mode and content of the address. No sensible person could say tawḥīd and shirk are equally true, so it is certain that one of the two is on the path of truth and the other in error — *now it is up to you. You think, and you decide who is on the side of truth. Is it we, or is it you?*

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains the reason: had the addressee been called a disbeliever or someone off the track of truth, it could have made him angry. That approach was avoided, and in its place "the approach was kept so affectionate and disarming that it would make even the most diehard adversary left with no choice but to consider what was being proposed" (from Qurtubi and Bayan-ul-Qurʼan). This is the Qur'an's own command in practice: *and argue with them in the best manners* (16:125) — something the ʿulamāʼ should keep in sight all the time. And the warning is blunt: once this stands ignored, everything done in the fair name of daʿwah, tablīgh and debate becomes ineffective, rather harmful — because adversaries turn adamant and cling to their error far more firmly.

## Ayat 25–26: parting ways, and who decides

*Say: You will not be accountable for our misdeeds, nor will we be accountable for what you do.* Ibn Kathir says this indicates **disowning them**: you do not belong to us and we do not belong to you. He frames the reason: because we call people to Allah, to believe that He is the only true deity and to worship Him alone. "If you respond, then you will belong to us and we to you, but if you reject our call, then we have nothing to do with you and you have nothing to do with us." The door stays open; the separation only takes effect on their refusal. He cites the parallels: *For me are my deeds and for you are your deeds! You are innocent of what I do, and I am innocent of what you do* (10:41), and *Say: O disbelievers! … To you be your religion, and to me my religion* (109:1–6).

Notice too the courtesy in the wording of ayah 25. Our side's actions are named as *our sins*; theirs merely as *what you do*. Even in separating, the harsher word is turned inward.

Ayah 26 says where the disagreement is finally settled: *Our Lord will gather us together, then He will judge between us with the truth.* Ibn Kathir: on the Day of Resurrection He will bring all of creation together in one arena, then judge between them with truth, that is, with justice — each person rewarded or punished according to his deeds; if they are good, his end will be good, and if they are bad, his end will be bad. On that Day they will know who has attained victory, glory and eternal happiness. He cites: *And on the Day when the Hour will be established — that Day shall all men be separated. Then as for those who believed and did righteous good deeds, such shall be honoured and made to enjoy a luxurious life for ever in a Garden of Delight. And as for those who disbelieved and denied Our Ayat, and the meeting of the Hereafter, such shall be brought forth to the torment* (30:14–16).

The ayah closes with two names: *He is **al-Fattāḥ al-ʿAlīm*** — rendered by Ibn Kathir as "the Just Judge, the All-Knower of the true state of affairs." He judges knowing exactly how things stand, so nothing can be argued past Him.

There is real relief in this ayah for anyone carrying an unresolved argument about the truth. You are not required to force the verdict now. State the case, live it, and leave the judging to the One who will gather everyone and knows the true state of affairs.

## Ayah 27: show me

The case ends with a challenge: *Say: Show me those you have joined with Him as partners.* Ibn Kathir: show me those gods whom you made as rivals and equals to Allah. **Arūnī** — produce them. After ayat 22–23 have emptied them of ownership, partnership, support and influence, there is nothing left to point at.

Then comes **kallā** — "Nay." Ibn Kathir: He has no peer, rival, partner or equal. And in place of the emptiness: *But He is Allah* — meaning, says Ibn Kathir, the One and Only Deity Who has no partner — ***al-ʿAzīz al-Ḥakīm***, the Almighty, the All-Wise: "the Owner of might with which He subjugates and controls all things, the One Who is Wise in all His Words and deeds, Laws and decrees." Might without wisdom would be terrifying; wisdom without might would be helpless. He is both. "Blessed and exalted and sanctified be He far above all that they say."

## Living it

**Locate your hope accurately.** The third group in ayah 22 were not crude idolaters; they simply believed that access mattered. Ayah 23 answers that permanently: intercession benefits no one except by Allah's permission, and even the Prophet ﷺ, the greatest intercessor, receives it from prostration. So bring your needs directly to the One who owns them.

**Let the unseen resize you.** Ayah 23 and the report from Abu Hurayrah show angels overcome by a single divine command, beating their wings with a sound like a chain on smooth rock, so shaken that they ask one another afterwards what was said — and then transmitting it without adding or taking away anything. Set your own casual relationship with Allah's words beside that.

**Argue like ayah 24.** Bring the proof, then leave the person their dignity and their decision. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's warning is the measure of how seriously the Qur'an takes this: daʿwah conducted without this courtesy does not merely fail, it hardens people in the very error you were trying to lift.

passages.title: A warner to all, and the appointed Day
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat move from the scope of the Prophet's ﷺ mission to the certainty of the Day he was sent to warn about. In ayah 28 Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ that he was sent to **all** people, as a bearer of glad tidings and a warner — yet most people do not know. In ayah 29 the deniers throw back a mocking question: *when* is this promise you keep threatening us with? And in ayah 30 the answer comes: you have an appointment, on a fixed Day, and you cannot shift it by a single hour in either direction. What holds the passage together is the logic of warning: a universal warner has been sent, most people ignore him, they demand a timetable — and they are told that the appointment is real and unmovable, which is precisely why the warning matters now.

## Where this comes in the surah

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out the connection to what came before: the previous verses were establishing that Allah is One and that His power is absolute. Ayah 28 then follows on — Allah has sent His Messenger ﷺ to all the peoples of the world, those who are there now and those who will come in the future.

## "Kāffatan li'n-nās" — the word placed early on purpose

The heart of ayah 28 is the phrase **كَافَّةً لِّلنَّاسِ** (*kāffatan li'n-nās*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *kāffah* carries the sense of making something universal and inclusive of all, without anyone being excluded from it. Grammatically, *kāffah* here is a **ḥāl** — Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it an adverb — relating to *an-nās*, "the people". By the ordinary grammatical arrangement you would therefore expect **لِلنَّاسِ كَافَّةً** (*li'n-nāsi kāffatan*), "for the people as a whole".

But the Qur'an sets *kāffah* to come earlier. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads that placement as deliberate: bringing "all" forward puts a clear accent on the universality of the mission of the Last Rasul of Allah ﷺ. The very first thing you hear in the phrase is *everyone*.

Ibn Kathir glosses "to all mankind" as meaning **to all of creation among those who are accountable for their deeds**, and cites two parallel ayat that say the same thing: *"Say: O mankind! Verily, I am sent to you all as the Messenger of Allah"* (7:158), and *"Blessed be He Who sent down the Criterion to His servant that he may be a warner to all creatures"* (25:1). Among the early authorities, Muḥammad bin Kaʿb said simply that it means "to all the people." Qatādah said: "Allah, may He be exalted, sent Muhammad ﷺ to both the Arabs and the non-Arabs, so the most honoured of them with Allah is the one who is most obedient to Allah." That last clause is worth sitting with — the universality of the message is exactly what dissolves any claim of ethnic privilege within it. If everyone is addressed, then rank inside the message can only be earned by obedience.

## "Bashīran wa nadhīran" — the two halves of one message

**بَشِيرًا** (*bashīr*, a bringer of good news) and **نَذِيرًا** (*nadhīr*, a warner) are given together, and Ibn Kathir spells out what each points to: to bring the glad tidings of Paradise to those who obey you, and to warn of the fire of Hell to those who disobey you.

They are not two moods to choose between. A messenger who only cheered would leave people unprepared; one who only frightened would leave them without hope. Paradise for those who obey and the Fire for those who disobey are the two real destinations, so the message that announces them has to carry both notes at once.

## "But most people do not know"

The ayah ends on a sober note, and Ibn Kathir sets it beside two other statements of the same reality: *"And most of mankind will not believe even if you desire it eagerly"* (12:103), and *"And if you obey most of those on the earth, they will mislead you far away from Allah's path"* (6:116).

Placed right after the announcement of a universal mission, this is a striking pairing. The message is for everybody; most will not receive it. And the second of those cross-references adds a warning that has nothing to do with numbers being comforting: majority opinion is not a guide. If you took the position of most of the people of the earth as your compass, it would carry you away from Allah's path. The Messenger ﷺ was sent to all; his measure of success was never a headcount.

## Who exactly is "all"?

Ibn Kathir reports that it was also recorded in the Ṣaḥīḥ that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said, **"I have been sent to the black and the red."** On the meaning of that expression, Mujāhid said it means to the jinn and to mankind; others said it meant the Arabs and the non-Arabs. Ibn Kathir's verdict: **both meanings are correct.** This is a good example of how the scholars handled a phrase that legitimately carries more than one sense — rather than forcing a single reading, they let both stand where both are true.

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the same breadth along a second axis — time. The mission is not simply for human beings but for the jinn as well; and it is not just for those present during his blessed time, but is universally applicable to all human generations to come, right up to the last day of Qiyāmah.

## From the Sunnah: the five things

Both commentaries cite the same narration here, from Sayyidnā Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him), which Ibn Kathir reports as being **in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs** and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān names as appearing **in the Ṣaḥīḥs of al-Bukhārī and Muslim and elsewhere**. The Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that he was given five things not given to any prophet before him:

**1. "I have been aided by fear (the distance of) a month's journey."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains this as Allah placing in his person such an awe as is felt by people from the distance of a month of travel.

**2. "The entire earth has been made a masjid and a means of purification for me"** — so that when the time for prayer comes, any man of his Ummah should pray. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān fills in the contrast: in the religious codes of past prophets, worship used to be performed only in particular places set up as houses of worship; it was not allowed outside those appointed prayer places, either in the open or inside homes. For the Muslim community the whole earth was made a masjid in the sense that ṣalāh can be made everywhere — and where water is not available or its use would be harmful, the dust of the earth was made *ṭahūr*, a purifier, so that it can be used to make **tayammum** (purification using clean earth), which becomes a valid alternative to *wuḍūʼ*.

**3. "The spoils of war have been made permissible for me,"** whereas they were not permitted for any before him. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes the earlier practice: the rule among them was to assemble the war spoils collected from the disbelieving adversary and deposit them at an appointed place, in the belief that some fire or lightning would descend from the heavens and burn them, and that act of burning would itself be the sign that their religious war had been accepted. For the Muslim community, distributing the spoils in accordance with the rule enunciated by the Qur'an and spending them as needed was made permissible.

**4. "I have been given the power of intercession."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān identifies this as the station of **ash-Shafāʿah al-Kubrā**, the Great Intercession: when no prophet would dare intercede on behalf of others on the fateful plains of the Resurrection, he ﷺ will then be given the opportunity to intercede.

**5. "The Prophets before me were sent to their own people, but I have been sent to all of mankind."** This last one is the hadith's direct commentary on ayah 28 — which is why both commentaries bring the narration here.

Read as a set, the five are not a list of honours for their own sake. Four of them are the practical equipment of a universal mission: a message that must reach everywhere needs a prayer that can be performed everywhere and a purification that does not depend on finding water; a community that must move needs a lawful way to handle what it acquires; a Messenger ﷺ who answers for all mankind is granted a standing to intercede for them.

## Why a universal mission means a final one

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws a further conclusion from ayah 28, and the reasoning is worth following closely. The mission of every prophet sent before was restricted to some particular people and a particular geographical area; the peculiarity of Sayyidnā Muhammad al-Muṣṭafā ﷺ is that his prophetic mission is common and open to all peoples of the world. That very fact of the continuity and survival of his mission, it argues, demands that he be the Last and Final of the prophets, and that no prophet is to come after him.

Why? Because of *why* a new prophet was ever sent. Another prophet is sent when the law and teachings of the one before him are distorted or altered — sent to reform the people and reinstate them according to Allah's pleasure. But the Sharīʿah of the Prophet ﷺ and his Book, the Qur'an, are different in one decisive respect: Allah Taʿālā Himself has already undertaken the responsibility of protecting it right through the last day of Qiyāmah. It will therefore hold on and survive till Qiyāmah in its original state, and the reason that used to call for a new prophet will never arise again. Finality is not an arbitrary stopping point; it follows from the preservation of the revelation.

## Ayah 29: the mocking question

**وَيَقُولُونَ مَتَىٰ هَٰذَا الْوَعْدُ إِن كُنتُمْ صَادِقِينَ** — "And they say: *When is this promise if you are truthful?*"

Ibn Kathir reads this as Allah telling us how the disbelievers **believed it unlikely that the Hour would ever come to pass**. The question is not a request for information; it is a way of saying the thing will never happen.

Ibn Kathir sets this beside a verse that names the two opposite responses to the same news: *"Those who believe not therein seek to hasten it, while those who believe are fearful of it, and know that it is the very truth"* (42:18). The one who does not believe presses for the Hour to arrive, because pressing for it is a way of dismissing it. The believer knows it is true, and therefore approaches it with awe. Your reaction to the mention of that Day tells you where you actually stand.

## Ayah 30: an appointment you cannot move

**قُل لَّكُم مِّيعَادُ يَوْمٍ لَّا تَسْتَأْخِرُونَ عَنْهُ سَاعَةً وَلَا تَسْتَقْدِمُونَ** — "Say: The appointment to you is for a Day, which you cannot put back for an hour nor put forward."

The reply does not give a date. It gives something the questioner had not reckoned with: a **mīʿād**, an appointed time — a fixed engagement that they are party to. Ibn Kathir's paraphrase: 'you have an appointed time which is fixed and cannot be changed or altered. When it comes, you will not be able to put it back or bring it forward.'

Feel the shape of the denial. Both verbs are addressed directly to them — *lā tasta'khirūna*, you cannot put it back, and *lā tastaqdimūna*, you cannot bring it forward — and the Day is sealed at both ends. Not delayed by an hour, not advanced by an hour. Every human strategy for handling an unwelcome deadline is closed off in half a line. And so the mockery of ayah 29 collapses: they asked *when*, assuming that not knowing the date meant there was no date. The answer is that the date is set, is not theirs to negotiate, and their ignorance of it changes nothing about it.

Ibn Kathir supports this with two more ayat: *"Verily, the term of Allah when it comes, cannot be delayed"* (71:4), and *"And We delay it only for a term already fixed. On the Day when it comes, no person shall speak except by His leave. Some among them will be wretched and (others) blessed"* (11:104–105). The second adds two details that answer the taunting tone of ayah 29 exactly. On that Day nobody speaks except by Allah's permission — the voices that were so loud with questions will be silent unless permitted. And the crowd will divide into the wretched and the blessed: the very two outcomes that *bashīran wa nadhīran* in ayah 28 was sent to announce. The passage closes the circle it opened.

## Living it

**Take the warner seriously in your own case.** The mission described in ayah 28 includes you — not because of your language or lineage, but because, as Ibn Kathir puts it, it reaches all of creation among those who are accountable for their deeds. Qatādah's remark is the practical version: whatever your background, closeness to Allah is measured by obedience.

**Hold the good news and the warning together.** Ayah 28 pairs them; an inner life built on only one of them is unbalanced. Hope without fear breeds carelessness; fear without hope breeds despair.

**Do not use numbers as a measure of truth.** "Most people do not know" is stated as a fact, not a complaint — and 6:116, which Ibn Kathir cites here, warns that obeying most of those on the earth would mislead you far away from Allah's path.

**Let the fixedness of the appointment work on you the right way.** The lesson of ayah 30 is not anxiety about a date. It is that the deadline is real, unnegotiable, and undisclosed — so the only sane response is the one 42:18 describes of the believers: knowing it is the very truth, and living in awe of it now.

**Value the ease you were given.** The whole earth as a place of prayer, and clean earth as a purifier when water fails: the second of the five gifts is not a historical curiosity but a permission you use whenever you pray away from a masjid. Praying where you happen to be is itself part of what it means to belong to a universal mission.

passages.title: Leaders and followers trading blame before their Lord
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat take a single sentence of defiance spoken in this world and follow it all the way to its end. The disbelievers announce in ayah 31 that they will never believe in the Qur'an — and Allah immediately lifts the curtain on the Day when the same people will be standing before Him, no longer united in their denial but tearing at one another over who is to blame. What holds the passage together is that argument: three speeches (31, 32, 33) passing the blame back and forth, ending with a verdict that neither side can escape.

## The refusal, and the answer to it

Ibn Kathir opens by saying that Allah here tells us of "the excessive wrongdoing and stubbornness of the disbelievers, and their insistence on not believing in the Holy Qur'an and what it tells them about the Resurrection." Notice how precise that is. Their quarrel was not only with the Book; it was with what the Book told them about being raised and answering for themselves. So the reply Allah gives is not an argument — it is a scene. You deny the Resurrection? Then look at yourselves in it.

Notice too how wide they make their vow. It is not only this Qur'an they refuse, but **"nor in that which was before it."** They leave themselves no opening anywhere. That is the "insistence" and "stubbornness" Ibn Kathir names: a refusal stated in the broadest terms its speakers could find.

Then Allah says, in effect: *if only you could see*. Ibn Kathir reads this as a threat: "Allah threatens them and warns them of the humiliating position they will be in before Him, arguing and disputing with one another." Two words in that sentence carry the weight. **Humiliating** — because the scene is not merely painful, it is degrading; and **before Him**, standing where nothing can be spun. In this world their denial looked like strength, a united front. There it becomes a squabble.

## "They will cast the blaming word one to another"

Feel the picture in the wording: they *cast the blaming word one to another*. The verse does not say they discuss, or complain, or petition. The word itself goes back and forth between them, thrown and returned. It is the sound of a collapsed alliance.

## Two names for two crowds

Ibn Kathir identifies the two parties with a minimum of words, and the identification is the key to everything that follows.

**Those who were deemed weak** — of these Ibn Kathir says plainly that this "refers to the followers."

**Those who were arrogant** — of these he says it "refers to the leaders and masters."

That is the shape of the argument that follows. The followers will plead that something was done to them; the leaders will insist that nothing was ever forced on anyone.

## Round one — the followers (ayah 31)

**"Had it not been for you, we should certainly have been believers!"** Ibn Kathir gives their meaning: "if you had not stopped us, we would have followed the Messengers and believed in what they brought."

Read that carefully and you will notice it is a claim about a life that never happened. It is not repentance. It is an alibi. And it is the oldest one there is: I would have been a different person, if only the people around me had been different.

## Round two — the leaders (ayah 32)

**"Did we keep you back from guidance after it had come to you?"** The question is thrown back as a question — and it lands, because it contains a fact the followers cannot deny: guidance *had come to them*. It arrived. It was in their hands.

Ibn Kathir puts the leaders' case in the first person, and it is uncomfortably strong: "we did nothing more to you than to call you, and you followed us without any evidence or proof, and you went against the evidence and proof which the Messengers brought because of your own desires; it was your own choice."

Four things are packed into that. The leaders only *called*; the followers came along with no evidence or proof; the Messengers *did* bring evidence and proof; and what tipped the followers was **their own desires**. Which is why the leaders end with **"Nay, but you were criminals"** — wrongdoers in your own right, not victims of ours.

It is a hard thing to sit with: on this one point, the arrogant are telling the truth. Following a liar is not an excuse when the truth was standing there with its proofs, and what made the liar attractive was what you already wanted.

## Round three — the followers again (ayah 33)

They will not accept it. **"Nay, but it was your plotting by night and day."** Ibn Kathir explains their charge: "you used to plot against us night and day, tempting us with promises and false hopes, and telling us that we were truly guided and that we were following something, but all of that was falsehood and manifest lies."

That is a real description of how misguidance is sold: not by argument, but by flattery and false hope — *you are the guided ones, you are on something* — repeated relentlessly, day and night, until it feels like knowledge.

On the phrase itself, Ibn Kathir reports that **Qatadah and Ibn Zayd** said it means "You plotted by night and day," and that **Malik narrated something similar from Zayd bin Aslam**. Read that way, the accusation is not about some quality belonging to the night and the day; it is about what these leaders *did*, and did without pause, through both.

Then comes the real indictment: **"when you ordered us to disbelieve in Allah and set up rivals to Him."** Ibn Kathir explains: "to set up gods as equal to Him, and you created doubts and confusion in our minds, and you fabricated far-fetched ideas with which to lead us astray." Three tools, in order: doubt, confusion, and elaborate far-fetched ideas. Shirk — associating anything with Allah as an equal to Him — rarely arrives announcing itself. It arrives as sophistication.

## The silence after the shouting

**"And each of them will conceal their own regrets, when they behold the torment."** The blaming stops, and what is left is not spoken aloud: the regret is kept inside. The torment has come into view, and there is nothing more to say to one another.

Ibn Kathir's comment is one line and it levels both parties: "both the leaders and the followers will feel regret for what they did previously." Not one side. Both. Every voice in the argument ends in the same swallowed regret — and note what the regret is over: **what they did**. In the end even the followers are left with their own record.

## The collars

**"And We shall put iron collars round the necks of those who disbelieved."** Ibn Kathir describes them concretely: "This is a chain which will tie their hands to their necks."

It is worth pausing on the aptness of it. Hands bound to the neck, and the arguing is over — you cannot point a finger when your hands are chained under your chin.

## "Are they requited aught except what they used to do?"

This closing question is the verdict of the whole passage. Ibn Kathir: "they will be punished according to their deeds: the leaders will be punished according to what they did, and the followers will be punished according to what they did."

That is the answer to the entire quarrel. The argument in ayat 31–33 assumes there is a fixed amount of blame to be divided, so that if one side carries it the other is lighter. There is no such pool. Each party is repaid for its own record. Misleading is a deed; being led is a deed. Nobody's file is opened as a subtraction from someone else's.

Ibn Kathir sets alongside this a verse from Surah al-Aʿraf, where Allah says: **"For each one there is double (torment), but you know not"** (7:38). *But you know not* — they did not know, on the day they were plotting or the day they were following, what they were building.

## From the Sunnah

Ibn Kathir closes on this passage with a narration: **Ibn Abi Hatim recorded that Abu Hurayrah**, may Allah be pleased with him, said that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said that when the people of Hell are driven towards it, it will meet them with its flames, then the Fire will burn their faces and the flesh will all fall to their hamstrings.

He brings it here for a reason. The passage has just described people who denied precisely this — "we will never believe in this Qur'an" — and Ibn Kathir told us at the outset that what they were refusing was what the Book told them about the Resurrection. The narration is the concrete shape of the thing they said would never come.

## Living it

The passage is a warning, and its practical edge is sharp in three directions.

**Do not build your faith on people.** The excuse in ayah 31 — *had it not been for you* — will be refused. If your religion rests on a personality, a movement, a teacher, or a family's approval, then the same crowd that carries you now will be arguing with you there. Faith has to be *yours*: known, chosen, held.

**Test what you are being told, especially when it flatters you.** The followers' complaint in ayah 33 is that they were fed "promises and false hopes" and told they "were truly guided." That is the exact sensation to be suspicious of. The Messengers came with evidence and proof; the leaders, by their own admission, did nothing more than call. Ask which one you are actually following.

**If you lead anyone, know what you are carrying.** Anyone with a voice — a parent, a teacher, an older sibling, someone with an audience — should read ayah 32 as the leaders' own account of themselves, and ayah 33 as the record kept of every night and day of it. The final question, *"Are they requited aught except what they used to do?"*, does not let a leader hide behind someone else's free choice any more than it lets a follower hide behind pressure. Both were doing something. Both will be handed back exactly that.

And the mercy hidden in all of it: this scene is shown to us *now*, while there is still time to change which side of the conversation we would be standing on.

passages.title: Wealth is no proof of Allah's favour
passages.tafsir:
**What this passage is about.** These six ayat answer one of the oldest arguments ever raised against a prophet. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān describes it: all along the lanes of time, people intoxicated with material wealth and luxury have opposed the voice of truth and taken a stance of hostility towards the prophets and the pious — except those whom Allah willed otherwise — and they would argue in favour of their own position by saying: *Had Allah disliked our doings and ways, why would He give us wealth, recognition and power in this world?* Allah answers that argument here — not by denying that He gave them wealth, but by denying that wealth was ever a certificate of His pleasure.

## The occasion of revelation: a merchant comes back from the coast

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān (citing Ibn Kathir and Mazhari) relates the incident behind these ayat. In the days of Jāhiliyyah, two men ran a business in partnership. Then one of them left and settled in some coastal area. When the Prophet ﷺ was made a prophet and people in Arabia started talking about it, the partner now living on the coast wrote to his old partner in Makkah, asking how people were responding to this man claiming to be a prophet. The reply came back: no one from among the Quraysh had followed him — only a few people of no consequence, mostly poor and needy.

The man of the coast had studied the older scriptures, the Torah and the Evangel. He left his business behind, came to Makkah, and presented himself before the Prophet ﷺ. He asked, "What is it to which you invite people to come?" The Prophet ﷺ told him about the main elements of his daʻwah of Islam. Immediately on hearing it he said: *Ashhadu annaka rasūl Allāh* — "I bear witness that you are, without any doubt, the Messenger of Allah." Asked how he knew this, he answered that as for the call being true, he had understood that through his own reason — and then the sign of it was this: the adherents of all the noble prophets who came earlier had, in the beginning, always been the weak and the meek, the poor and needy, people who did not matter much among those they were sent to.

And it was then that ayah 34 was revealed. The very fact the Makkan partner offered as *evidence against* the Prophet ﷺ is what this reader of scripture recognised as *evidence for* him.

## "Its elite" — the word *mutraf*

In ayah 34 the objectors are named with one word: **مُتْرَفُوهَا** (*mutrafūhā*). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that it comes from the root **تَرَف** (*taraf*), which carries the sense of a life abounding in material assets, ease and comfort. So *mutrafīn* denotes the rich people of a community — with the added colouring of arrogance and carelessness about what is right and wrong. Ibn Kathir glosses it as those who enjoyed a life of riches and luxury *and positions of leadership*: it is not wealth alone but wealth plus power. Qatādah put it bluntly: "They are their tyrants, chiefs and leaders in evil."

Note also the reach of the sentence: **"We did not send a warner to a township but…"** — the phrasing leaves no township out. The warner is a *nadhīr*, which Ibn Kathir notes means a Prophet or a Messenger. And ayah 34 has them say *"We believe not in the message with which you have been sent"* — which Ibn Kathir explains as: we do not believe in it and we will not follow it. A refusal of both heart and conduct.

## A pattern as old as prophethood

Ibn Kathir's headline observation is that **Allah is consoling His Prophet ﷺ**, commanding him to follow the example of the Messengers who came before him: no Prophet was ever sent to a township but those among its people who lived a life of luxury disbelieved in him, while the weaker people of the town followed him. He gathers the evidence from across the Qurʼān:

- The people of Nūḥ (peace be upon him): *"Shall we believe in you, when the weakest of the people follow you?"* (26:110), and *"nor do we see any follow you but the meanest among us"* (11:27).
- The leaders among the people of Ṣāliḥ: the arrogant said to those who were counted weak and had believed, *"Verily, we disbelieve in that which you believe in"* (7:75–76).
- *"Thus We have tried some of them with others, that they might say: 'Is it these poor believers that Allah has favoured from among us?'"* (6:53).
- *"And thus We have set up in every town great ones of its wicked people to plot therein"* (6:123).
- *"And when We decide to destroy a town, We first send a definite order to those among them who lead a life of luxury. Then they transgress therein, and thus the Word of torment is justified against it. Then We destroy it with complete destruction"* (17:16).

So for the Prophet ﷺ — and for anyone carrying truth into a room of the successful — resistance is not a sign that something has gone wrong. It is the standard shape of the encounter.

## The argument in ayah 35, and why it collapses

Ayah 35 gives their reasoning in two clauses: **"We are more in wealth and in children"** — and therefore **"we are not going to be punished."** Ibn Kathir explains that they were proud of their great wealth and great numbers of children, and believed that this was a sign that Allah loved them and cared for them: that if He gave them this in this world, He would not punish them in the Hereafter. Ibn Kathir's verdict on the inference is short — "this was too far-fetched." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān calls it the age-old satanic illusion of taking worldly riches and honours as proof of being loved by Allah.

Ibn Kathir answers with the Qurʼān's own repeated corrections of this illusion:

- *"Do they think that in the wealth and children with which We enlarge them We hasten unto them good things? Nay, but they perceive not"* (23:55–56).
- *"So let not their wealth nor their children amaze you; in reality Allah's plan is to punish them with these things in the life of this world, and that their souls shall depart while they are disbelievers"* (Sūrah at-Tawbah).
- The man of Sūrah al-Muddaththir, granted resources in abundance, children to be by his side and a life made smooth and comfortable, who then desires still more: *"Nay! Verily, he has been opposing Our signs. I shall oblige him to face a severe torment"* (74:11–17).

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out how wealth can itself be the punishment: people become so involved in and infatuated with wealth and property that they never find the time to think about their ultimate fate or turn towards Allah and the Hereafter — and within this world, for the sake of wealth and children, they have to suffer thousands of distresses and pains. Their punishment starts taking effect right from this very world.

## Ayah 36: He expands and He restricts

The answer opens with **قُلْ** — "Say." *"Verily, my Lord expands the provision to whom He wills and restricts."* Ibn Kathir's comment cuts the objectors' logic at the root: **He gives wealth to those whom He loves and to those whom He does not love**, and He makes poor whom He wills and makes rich whom He wills; He has complete wisdom and clear proof. Hence the close of the ayah: **"but most men know not."**

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān puts the same point positively: having more wealth and recognition in this world, or not having any, is no proof of someone being acceptable or unacceptable in the sight of Allah. It is in view of creational considerations that He gives property and wealth in abundance to whomever He wills, and less to whomever He wills — and He alone knows the consideration behind it. To take an abundance of wealth and children as proof of being acceptable to Allah is, in Maʿārif's words, sheer ignorance.

## Ayah 37: what actually brings you near

**"And it is not your wealth, nor your children that bring you nearer to Us"** — Ibn Kathir: meaning, these things are not a sign that We love you or care for you.

Ibn Kathir cites here the ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) recorded by Imam Aḥmad — and also by **Muslim** and **Ibn Mājah** — that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "Allah does not look at your outward appearance or your wealth, rather He looks at your hearts and your deeds."

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same narration of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) and attributes it to Aḥmad and Ibn Kathir.

Then comes the exception: **"but only he who believes and does righteous deeds."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the point in ledger terms — with Allah the criterion of acceptability, approval, support and pleasure is no other than *īmān* (faith) and good deeds; one who does not carry these two assets cannot be made acceptable by any quantity of wealth or children.

**The multiplied reward.** *"For such there will be jazāʼ aḍ-ḍiʿf for what they did."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that **ضِعْف** (*ḍiʿf*, with a kasrah on the ḍād) is a verbal noun meaning "like a thing" or "the likes of a thing." Just as wealthy people keep amassing their wealth in this worldly life, Allah increases the return for His accepted servants in the Hereafter many times over — the return for one deed being ten of its likes, and, given the person's sincerity and other causes and considerations, up to seven hundred times, which Maʿārif notes stands proved from ṣaḥīḥ aḥādīth; and even that is not a restriction — it could be more. Ibn Kathir says the same: the reward will be multiplied for them between ten and seven hundred times. And Maʿārif adds that this holds whether or not such people were ever recognised in this world. The believers' reply to the boast of ayah 35 is not that accumulation is meaningless — it is that they are accumulating in the market that stays open.

**The high chambers.** *"And they will reside in the ghurufāt in peace and security."* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that **غُرُفَات** (*ghurufāt*) is the plural of **غُرْفَة** (*ghurfah*), which denotes a part of a mansion considered distinct and high compared with the other parts. Ibn Kathir: the lofty dwellings of Paradise, safe from all misery, fear and harm. Set that word beside *mutraf*: the passage does not deny anyone a mansion — it relocates it.

Ibn Kathir cites what **Ibn Abī Ḥātim** recorded from ʻAlī (may Allah be pleased with him), that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said:

> "In Paradise there are lofty rooms whose outside can be seen from the inside and whose inside can be seen from the outside."

A bedouin asked, "Who are they for?" He ﷺ said:

> "For those who speak well, feed the hungry, persist in fasting, and pray at night while people are asleep."

Four qualities: a good tongue, a generous hand, a disciplined appetite, a private life with Allah. None of them requires wealth.

## Ayah 38: the other side

**"And those who strive against Our signs, to frustrate them."** Ibn Kathir explains this of those who try to block people from the path of Allah, from following His Messengers, and from believing in His signs. A step beyond mere disbelief: an active campaign. *"Those will be brought to the torment"* — and Ibn Kathir adds the note of exact justice: they will all be punished for their deeds, **each one accordingly**.

## Ayah 39: the same words, a different audience

Ayah 39 repeats ayah 36 almost word for word, with two small additions: **مِنْ عِبَادِهِ** ("of His servants") after "whom He wills," and **لَهُ** ("for him") after "restricts." Maʿārif ul Qurʼān treats these as the key to why the sentence comes twice.

**First**, from "of His servants" it is gathered that this rule of guidance has been put forth for Allah's particular servants — that is, for the believers — and the purpose is to alert the people of faith that they should not begin loving wealth and comfort to the extent that their hearts choke when it comes to spending on the occasions and the rights that Allah has enjoined. The earlier ayah 36 was addressed to the disbelievers and polytheists who prided themselves on the worldly assets of wealth and children. So the two addresses are different, and no discordance remains. Maʿārif notes that Maulānā Ashraf ʻAlī Thānavī, in his *khulāṣah* of Tafsīr Bayān ul-Qurʼān, took the same approach, first adding "the believers" in parenthesis when explaining this ayah. So the passage does not let the reader stand comfortably on the side of the poor believers and enjoy the rebuke of the rich. It comes for the believer's own grip on his money.

**Second**, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports that some commentators point to a different distinction: ayah 36 mentions the distribution of sustenance *between different human beings* — more to some, less to others, all in His wisdom — while ayah 39, with its "for him," mentions *one person and his different states*: at times this same person has more with him, and at another time much less. Either reading leaves no redundancy between the two ayat.

Ibn Kathir's comment on this second statement is that, according to His wisdom, He gives a lot of provision to one and very little to another, and He has great wisdom in doing so which cannot be comprehended by anyone but Him. Ibn Kathir pairs this with *"See how We favour one above another, and verily the Hereafter will be greater in degrees and greater in favour"* (17:21): just as there are differences between people in this world, so they will be in the Hereafter, where one will reside in apartments in the highest levels of Paradise while another will be in the lowest levels of Hell. The difference is that *there* the ranking is by faith and deeds, and it is final.

And Ibn Kathir quotes here the Prophet ﷺ describing the best of people in this world, in a narration **recorded by Muslim**:

> "He truly succeeds who becomes Muslim, and is given just enough provision, and Allah makes him content with what He has given."

## "And whatever you spend, He will replace it"

**"And whatever thing you spend, He replaces it — and He is the best of providers."**

Ibn Kathir: whatever you spend in the ways that He has commanded you and permitted you, He will compensate you for it — in this world by giving you something else instead, and in the Hereafter by giving you reward. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points to the pattern already visible in creation: water comes down from above, humans and animals use it freely, the needs of farms and forests are met, and no sooner is that supply used up than another descends to replenish it. In short, whatever a person spends, it is Allah's customary practice to replace it with something similar — and something happening contrary to this as an exceptional case, whether to punish someone or for the sake of some other creational consideration, is not to be deemed contrary to that customary practice.

**From the Sunnah on spending**, as the sources cite it:

- Ibn Kathir reports that the Prophet ﷺ said that Allah says: **"Spend, and I will spend on you."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports the same teaching: "Allah has told me: You spend on people, I shall spend on you."
- Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a ḥadīth of Abū Hurayrah (may Allah be pleased with him) in the **Ṣaḥīḥ of Muslim**: every day when people rise to another morning, two angels descend from the heavens and pray, "O Allah, bless the one who spends with its return, and let the one who withholds find it wasted." Ibn Kathir reports the same two angels, one saying, "O Allah, bring destruction upon the one who withholds," and the other, "O Allah, give compensation to the one who spends."
- Ibn Kathir reports that the Messenger of Allah ﷺ said: **"Spend, O Bilāl, and do not fear that the One Who is on the Throne will withhold from you."**

**A limit on the promise.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān cites a ḥadīth of Jābir (may Allah be pleased with him), reported by ad-Darqutni and Qurtubi: a good deed is *ṣadaqah*; what someone spends on himself or on his children and family also falls under *ṣadaqah* and brings *thawāb* (reward from Allah); and what one spends to protect his integrity and honour is *ṣadaqah* too. Whoever spends in obedience to the command of Allah, Allah has taken it upon Himself to give him its return — **except** what is spent on wasteful building beyond need, or in sinful activity: for that there is no promise of a return. When his disciple Ibn al-Munkadir asked what "spending to protect one's honour" meant, Jābir explained: there may be a person about whom one fears that, if he is not given something, he will go about maligning him in all sorts of ways — giving to such a person is in order to save one's honour.

## Living it

- **Stop reading a bank balance as a verdict.** Ibn Kathir's line is the cure: Allah gives wealth to those whom He loves and to those whom He does not love.
- **Check what you resent.** If a truth becomes less attractive to you because of who holds it, that is the disease this passage exposes.
- **Move your accumulation.** Ayah 37 does not ask you to stop wanting more; it tells you where "more" is multiplied from ten to seven hundred times and beyond.
- **Read ayah 39 as addressed to you.** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān's point is that the believer is the intended hearer of the repetition: the test is whether the heart chokes when it is time to give.
- **Spend lawfully.** The promised replacement attaches to what Allah commanded and permitted — including provision for your own family — not to wasteful building or sin.

passages.title: Angels disown those who worshipped them
passages.tafsir:
These three ayat put us inside a scene on the Day of Resurrection: Allah gathers them all together, turns to the angels, and asks them a single devastating question about the people who used to worship them. The angels' answer, and the verdict that follows, dismantle the whole logic of idolatry in a few lines.

What holds the passage together is its shape: a **question** (ayah 40), an **answer** (ayah 41), and a **sentence passed** (ayah 42). Nothing is argued abstractly. The false gods are simply brought face to face with their worshippers in public, and the case collapses on its own.

## Who did the idolaters think they were worshipping?

Ibn Kathir supplies the background that makes the question in ayah 40 land. The idolaters he is describing did not think of themselves as worshipping lifeless stone. They claimed **their idols were in the form of these angels**, and that through them they could **be brought nearer to Allah**. That is worth pausing on, because it means the idolatry here did not present itself as a rejection of Allah at all. It presented itself as a way of getting closer to Him. The images were, in their minds, honoured go-betweens.

So Allah does not begin by refuting the theology. He calls the alleged intercessors as witnesses.

## Ayah 40 — the question

**"And ˹consider˺ the Day He will gather them all together"** — *wa yawma yaḥshuruhum jamīʿan*. Ibn Kathir's summary of the scene is that on that Day Allah **"will rebuke the idolators before all of creation."** The rebuke is not private. It happens in front of everyone.

Then the question: **"Was it you that these people used to worship?"** Notice who is addressed. Allah does not begin with the guilty; He asks the angels.

Ibn Kathir explains what the question is really driving at: **"did you command them to worship you?"** That is, the excuse of the idolater is being tested at its root. If a heavenly authority told you to do this, let that authority speak now. Ibn Kathir places two parallel scenes beside it:

- Allah's question in Sūrat al-Furqān to the false objects of worship: *"Was it you who misled these My servants or did they (themselves) stray from the (right) path?"* (25:17).
- Allah's question to ʿĪsā, peace be upon him: *"Did you say unto men: 'Worship me and my mother as two gods besides Allah?'"* — and his answer, *"Glory be to You! It was not for me to say what I had no right (to say)"* (5:116).

The pattern is unmistakable, and Ibn Kathir draws it out himself: the same question is put to the angels and to ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, and the same answer comes back. The devotion was never authorised by the one it was directed at.

## Ayah 41 — the angels' answer

Their reply has three movements, and Ibn Kathir opens each one.

**First, they clear Allah's honour before they clear their own.** *Subḥānaka* — "Glorified be You!" Ibn Kathir glosses it: **"exalted and sanctified be You above the notion that there could be any god besides You."** Look at what this reveals about the angels. Accused of receiving worship, their first instinct is not self-defence but insistence on Allah's absolute exaltedness. It is the same word ʿĪsā, peace be upon him, uses in 5:116 when the same question is put to him. Ibn Kathir explicitly links the two: "Similarly, the angels will say: *Subḥānaka*."

**Second, they name where their own loyalty lies.** *Anta waliyyunā min dūnihim* — "You are our Protector instead of them." Ibn Kathir's paraphrase is: **"we are Your servants and we disown these people before You."** There is something quietly shattering in this. The angels do not merely deny commanding the worship; they disown the relationship altogether, and they do it *before Allah* — a public separation. And notice how they describe themselves: *Your servants*. That is the whole of their answer about their own standing.

**Third, they identify who was actually being served.** *"Nay, but they used to worship the Jinn; most of them were believers in them."* This is the turn in the passage. Ibn Kathir explains "the Jinn" here as **the Shayāṭīn** — the devils — **"because they are the ones who made idol worship attractive to them and who misguided them."**

Take that in. The worshipper thought he was addressing an angel. According to Ibn Kathir's reading, the party actually behind the act was the one who dressed it up and made it look appealing. Ibn Kathir places alongside it the ayah: *"They invoke nothing but females besides Him, and they invoke nothing but Shayṭān, a persistent rebel! Allah cursed him"* (4:117–118) — where invoking idols and invoking Shayṭān are spoken of together.

And *"most of them were believers in them"* is the sting. Whatever they thought their devotion was, their credence had been given to the very party that misguided them — while the beings they thought they were honouring were, all along, going to disown them.

## Ayah 42 — the verdict

**"So Today neither of you can benefit or protect each other"** — in Ibn Kathir's rendering, **"So Today, none of you can profit or harm one another."**

His comment goes straight to the psychology of it: **"none of those idols and rivals whom you hoped would benefit you, will be of any avail to you, those whom you worshipped in the hope that they would help you at times of stress and calamity. Today they will have no power either to benefit you or to harm you."**

Two things are worth sitting with here.

The first is *when* people had turned to these gods: **at times of stress and calamity**. That is when a false object of worship earns its keep — the emergency, the illness, the failing business, the night of fear. The exposure in ayah 42 comes at the ultimate emergency, and it is there that the whole arrangement pays out nothing.

The second is the pairing Ibn Kathir keeps intact: **neither benefit nor harm**. The hope was that these could do you good; the ayah denies them both the power to help and the power to hurt. Nothing is left of the arrangement in either direction. And the wording is mutual — "none of you can profit or harm one another" — so the emptiness runs both ways between worshipper and worshipped.

Then the closing rebuke: **"And We shall say to those who did wrong"** — Ibn Kathir: **"meaning the idolators"** — **"Taste the torment of the Fire which you used to deny."** The clause **"which you used to deny"** ties the punishment to the exact thing they had rejected as untrue. And Ibn Kathir notes the tone in which it is said: **"by way of rebuke."** The words are part of the reckoning, not merely information.

## Living it

The passage is not an antique quarrel about statues. Its logic reaches anyone.

**No creature can authorise the devotion you give it.** When the question is put — the angels here, and in the parallel Ibn Kathir cites, ʿĪsā, peace be upon him — the answer is the same: *Subḥānaka*. Note also what the idolaters had actually claimed: that these could **bring them nearer to Allah**. The passage takes that claim and answers it with rebuke and disownment.

**Notice who you actually turn to in a crisis.** Ibn Kathir's line about seeking help "at times of stress and calamity" is a mirror worth holding up. The instinctive move in a moment of panic tells you where the heart has quietly lodged its hope, whatever the tongue professes.

**Say *Subḥānaka* the way the angels say it.** For them it is not a phrase but a reflex — the first thing out of them under questioning is Allah's exaltedness, before any word about themselves. That is worth borrowing.

**Learn from how the angels describe themselves.** *Anta waliyyunā min dūnihim* — "You are our Protector instead of them" — which Ibn Kathir unpacks as *we are Your servants*. Their security is in knowing exactly whose they are. To have Allah as one's Protector is at the same time to be free of every lesser protector whose protection was never real.

passages.title: Calling clear revelation magic and invention
passages.tafsir:
This passage records what the disbelievers said when the Qur'an was recited to them — three dismissals in a row — and then answers them. What holds ayat 43–45 together is a single movement: their words, and then two replies from Allah. The first reply takes away the grounds on which they were judging (44); the second shows them the end of stronger nations who judged the same way (45).

Ibn Kathir frames the whole unit in one sentence: "Allah tells us that the disbeliever deserve to be severely punished by Him, because when His clear Verses were recited to them, and they heard them fresh from the lips of His Messenger ﷺ, they said…" Note the aggravating detail he draws out. This was not hearsay reaching them second-hand. They heard the revelation directly from the mouth of the Prophet ﷺ, and still spoke as they did.

## Three dismissals, and who was making them

The ayah sets two descriptions of the same recitation side by side. Allah calls what was recited **Our clear revelations**; the listeners call it an invented lie and evident magic. That contrast is the engine of the passage, and each of their three statements attacks something different.

**"This is naught but a man who wishes to hinder you from that which your fathers used to worship."** They do not engage the recitation; they profile the reciter. He is reduced to *a man* with a motive, and the motive they assign him is the one most likely to alarm their listeners — he wants to pull you away from your fathers. Ibn Kathir draws out the assumption buried inside the accusation: "that the religion of their fathers was the truth and that what the Messenger brought to them was false." Ancestral practice is treated as the fixed point, and revelation is measured against it rather than the reverse. Ibn Kathir's reaction to that inversion is unsparing: "may the curse of Allah be upon them and their fathers!"

**"This is nothing but an invented lie."** Ibn Kathir notes plainly that this is said "referring to the Qur'an." The charge has now moved from the man to the message: what he recites is a human composition with a human author.

**"This is nothing but evident magic!"** Here the wording of the ayah itself is worth pausing over, because Allah does not simply report the sentence. He reports it as spoken *of the truth when it has come to them*. In one breath the object of their judgement is named by Allah as **the truth** and by them as magic.

And then, before any argument is made, Allah identifies the people issuing this verdict:

**"And We had not given them Scriptures that they could study, nor sent to them before you any warner."**

Ibn Kathir's explanation is direct: "Allah did not reveal any Book to the Arabs before the Qur'an, and He did not send any Prophet to them before Muhammad ﷺ."

Feel the force of this placed next to their three statements. To pronounce a recited text an invented lie, or its reciter a sorcerer, you need some standard of comparison — a scripture you have studied, an earlier warner whose teaching you can hold this up against. They had neither. Their confident religious verdict rested on nothing but the inherited custom their own first objection had already put on display: what our fathers used to worship. They were not scholars detecting a forgery. They were people who had never been given a scripture, ruling on the only scripture ever sent to them.

## The very thing they had asked for

Ibn Kathir then adds the detail that turns the argument into a tragedy: "They used to wish for that and say, 'if only a warner comes to us or a Book is revealed to us, we would be more guided than others,' but when Allah blessed them with that, they disbelieved him and stubbornly rejected him."

They had asked for this. They had made it a boast — give us what the earlier nations were given and we will outdo them in guidance. Then a Book was revealed and a warner arose among them, and the same tongues that had made the wish said *invented lie* and *evident magic*. So ayah 44 is not only saying "you have no basis for this verdict." It is saying: this is the very thing you claimed you were waiting for.

## Stronger nations said it first

**"And those before them denied"** — Ibn Kathir: "meaning, other nations." The rejection recorded in ayah 43 is not original. It is a repetition, and the outcome of the earlier attempts is a matter of record.

**"these have not received even a tenth of what We had granted to those (of old)."** Maarif ul Quran records a genuine difference among the commentators over how far the word *mi'shar* reaches. It "has been taken to mean: 'ushr (a tenth) by some early commentators. Some scholars have interpreted it as: 'ushr-ul-'ushr (a hundredth) while others call it: 'ushr-ul-'ashir (a thousandth)." Maarif observes that this last reading carries the higher degree of emphasis, and sums up the ayah accordingly: "not even a tenth, rather a thousandth, of the worldly wealth, power, blessings of age and health given to earlier communities was received by the people of Makkah."

A tenth *of what*, exactly? Ibn Kathir answers with the early authorities. Ibn 'Abbas (may Allah be pleased with him) said, "Of the power of this world," and Ibn Kathir records that this was also the view of Qatadah, As-Suddi and Ibn Zayd. So the comparison is not one of spiritual standing but of sheer worldly strength — and, as Maarif adds, of length of life and health as well.

The argument is therefore one of proportion. The Makkans were secure enough in their own standing to dismiss a man reciting verses. Allah tells them they do not hold a tenth — or a hundredth, or a thousandth — of what the destroyed nations held. Whatever confidence their position gave them, those nations had more of it, and it did not save them.

Ibn Kathir supports this by setting two other ayat alongside. Of an earlier people Allah says: *"And indeed We had firmly established them with that wherewith We have not established you! And We had assigned them the hearing, seeing, and hearts; but their hearing, seeing, and their hearts availed them nothing since they used to deny the Ayat of Allah, and they were completely encircled by that which they used to mock at!"* (46:26). Faculties they certainly had — ears, eyes, hearts — and those faculties did them no good once they were turned against the signs of Allah; the very thing they had mocked closed in around them. And Allah asks: *"Have they not traveled through the earth and seen what was the end of those before them? They were more in number than them and mightier in strength"* (40:82). Ibn Kathir's comment: "but that did not protect them from the punishment of Allah, and Allah destroyed them because they denied His Messengers."

The passage then closes: **"yet they denied My Messengers. Then how (terrible) was My denial!"** Ibn Kathir renders it: "meaning, 'how severe was My wrath and how great was My avenging of My Messengers.'"

Two things in that closing line repay attention. First, Allah says **My** Messengers, and Ibn Kathir reads what followed as His avenging of them — the insult was not merely to a man from among their own people but to an envoy belonging to Allah. Second, ayah 44 spoke of a single *warner* sent to a single people, while ayah 45 speaks of *Messengers*, plural, denied by nations, plural. The quarrel at Makkah is placed inside a much older pattern, and the pattern has never once ended in the deniers' favour. And the closing words are put as a question — *how was My denial?* — a question anyone can answer by looking at what became of those nations.

## Living it

**A verdict needs grounds.** Ayah 44 disqualifies a judgement on revelation issued by people who had never been given a revelation to study. The discipline it asks of us is to know the difference between a considered position and an inherited reflex confidently expressed. It applies to how we speak about the Book of Allah, and to how we weigh what we are told about it by others.

**Inherited practice is not proof.** The first objection in ayah 43 treats "what your fathers used to worship" as the standard by which revelation is judged, and Ibn Kathir identifies exactly this as the error: taking their fathers' religion to be the truth and what the Messenger brought to be false. Love for one's forebears is one thing; making them the measure of truth is another.

**Do not ask for guidance you are unwilling to accept.** Ibn Kathir's note on ayah 44 — that they had wished aloud for a Book and a warner, and rejected both when they came — describes something more common than idolatry. Asking to be shown, and then resenting what we are shown, is a failing of ordinary religious life, not only of Quraysh.

**Read history as it is meant to be read.** Maarif ul Quran draws the practical conclusion from ayah 45 directly: "they should take lesson from what happened to past communities and the evil end they faced. These were people who invited upon themselves the wrath of Allah when they rejected prophets and messengers and, consequently, when came the actual punishment, their power, bravery, wealth and fortified fortresses could do nothing for them." Note the order in that sentence: the prophets came, they were rejected, and only then did the punishment arrive. That order is itself a mercy. Allah sent a warner before the reckoning — and the warning is still being recited.

passages.title: Stand up and reflect: I ask no reward
passages.tafsir:
## What this passage is

Five commands beginning **"Say"** (*qul*), one after another, addressed to the disbelievers of Makkah. Ibn Kathir opens the passage with its setting: Allah tells His Messenger ﷺ to speak to these disbelievers who claim that he is crazy. Each "Say" takes up a different piece — the single request he ﷺ puts to them (46), the question of any payment he might have wanted (47), where the truth he brings comes from (48), what has become of falsehood (49), and the source of his own guidance (50).

## Ayah 46 — the one piece of advice

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān notes that this ayah exists **to negate any excuse for the people of Makkah**: they are shown a shortcut to ascertain the truth, and asked to do just one thing.

**"Stand for Allah."** The word is *qiyām*, from the root of standing up. But Maʿārif ul Qurʼān is careful here: it does not mean standing in the physical sense, something like rising from sitting or lying down. It means *having the resolve to show full care and concern for the assignment in sight* — treating the question as serious and giving it your whole attention.

**"For Allah" (*lillāh*).** This is the condition that decides everything. Attaching *lillāh* to *qiyām*, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains, makes clear that one should start looking for truth **with a mind cleansed of previous thoughts and beliefs**, for the good pleasure of Allah alone, so that previous thoughts and deeds do not obstruct one's way to accepting the truth. Ibn Kathir says the same in his own words: *stand sincerely before Allah, without being influenced by your own desires or tribal feelings*. This is the heart of the ayah.

**"In pairs and singly" (*mathnā wa-furādā*).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān states that this expression is not intended to point out a particular number. It reads the phrase as naming the two ways a person can think a matter out: (1) to think it out alone and in private, and (2) to consult friends and elders, discuss it with them and then arrive at some conclusion — *and out of these two methods, you can go by the one you like*. Ibn Kathir's reading runs along the same lines: ask one another, "is Muhammad crazy?"; advise one another; and let each person look within himself concerning the matter, ask other people about him if he is still confused, and then think the matter over. Ibn Kathir adds that this meaning was stated by Mujahid, Muhammad bin Kaʿb, As-Suddi, Qatadah and others, and that this is what is meant by the ayah.

**"Then reflect" (*thumma tatafakkarū*).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān points out that the *thumma* ("then") refers back to *an taqūmū* ("that you stand"), where the purpose of standing has already been spelt out: cleanse your mind of all previous thoughts, get ready to act for the good pleasure of Allah — *then* think about the call of the Prophet ﷺ and decide for yourself whether or not it is true. The standing is not the goal; it is the preparation.

## The argument the ayah is inviting them into

Maʿārif ul Qurʼān lays out the line of thinking a person would follow. Look at the situation plainly: **here is a solitary person, all by himself**, with no power or group to back him and no wealth or property to strengthen him, coming forward to proclaim an article of faith counter to that of his own people — rather, of the whole world — something having taken firm roots over centuries and something they all agree to.

Such a proclamation, the commentary says, can come only in two forms:
