1. Either the person making it is totally insane, with no idea of his own gain or loss, ready to invite the wrath of his people and all sorts of hardship for himself; **or**
2. What he is saying might as well be true — that he is a *rasūl*, a messenger from Allah, and fears none in conveying and implementing His command.

Now, says Maʿārif ul Qurʼān, think hard with an open mind as to which of the two is the real thing. Think in that manner and you are left with no choice but to become certain that he cannot be insane. **The entire city of Makkah and everyone in the large tribe of Quraysh is aware of his wisdom and character.** He has spent forty years of his life among his people; from childhood to his youth, everything about him has been before them. No one has ever found any word or deed issuing forth from him to be counter to reason, wisdom, sobriety or gentleness. And other than the *kalimah* — *lā ilāha illa-llāh*, there is no god but Allah — to which he invites people, no one can doubt any of his word or deed to be counter to reason and wisdom, even today. So the first option collapses.

**"Your companion" (*ṣāḥibikum*).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws attention to this single word as releasing a hint in that direction. Should it be the case of a visitor coming in from outside, whose antecedents are unknown, who is heard saying something counter to the belief of a whole people, then it is possible to call him insane. But this cannot be true in his case: **he is one of you.** He lives in your city, he belongs to your brotherhood, he abides in your company be it day or night. Nothing he does is hidden from you. In fact — the point lands hard — *even you yourselves have never cast aspersions against him in that manner before this*.

And when the absence of the first situation becomes clear, the second stands established. Which is exactly what the ayah says next: **"He is none but a warner to you in the face of a stern torment."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān: his presence among them signifies nothing but that he has been sent there to save people from the severe punishment of the Day of Judgement by warning them of it in advance.

## From the Sunnah: the day on aṣ-Ṣafā

Al-Bukhari recorded that Ibn ʿAbbās, may Allah be pleased with him, commented on this ayah: one day the Prophet ﷺ climbed up aṣ-Ṣafā and shouted, *"Yā ṣabāḥāh!"* — rendered in the commentary as *"O people!"* The Quraysh gathered around him and said, "What is the matter with you?" He ﷺ said, **"What do you think? If I told you that the enemy were approaching and will reach us in the morning or in the evening, would you believe me?"** They said, "Of course." He ﷺ said, **"I am a warner to you in the face of a severe punishment."** Abu Lahab said, "May you perish! You have called us together only to tell us this?" Then Allah revealed, *"Perish the two hands of Abu Lahab and perish he!"* (111:1). Ibn Kathir notes that he has already discussed this in his commentary on *"And warn your tribe of near kindred"* (26:214).

Notice how the ayah's very phrase — *a warner to you in the face of a severe punishment* — is the wording the Prophet ﷺ used on the hill. And notice the comparison he ﷺ drew, which is the report's own: news of an enemy arriving by morning you would take on my word without hesitation.

## Ayah 47 — "whatever wage I might have asked of you is yours"

Ibn Kathir explains the meaning as: *I do not want anything for conveying the Message of Allah to you, advising you and telling you to worship Allah.* And *"my wage is from Allah only"* means: rather, I will seek the reward for that **with Allah**.

The phrasing is generous and disarming: whatever you imagine I have asked of you — keep it. The one motive people are quickest to suspect in a preacher is removed at a stroke. And the ayah closes on an attribute: **"He is a Witness over all things."** Ibn Kathir: He knows all things — He knows everything about me and the manner in which I am conveying the Message to you, and He knows all about you. The claim of sincerity is not left hanging on the Prophet's ﷺ word; it is submitted to the One who knows both sides of the exchange.

## Ayah 48 — how the truth arrives

**"Surely my Lord hurls the truth."** The verb is *yaqdhifu*, and Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the word: literally *qadhf* means **to hit by throwing**. My Lord, who is the Knower of the Unseen, strikes out the false with a throw of the truth. The commentary offers this cautiously — *perhaps* there is a wise consideration behind expressing the matter with this particular verb, namely to point to the after-effect of truth prevailing over the false. It appears, it says, in the form of a simile: the throwing of something heavy over something feeble, which shatters into pieces. So it happens in the confrontation between truth and falsehood, when the latter lies shattered. The commentary connects this to *"Nay, We fling the truth against the falsehood, so it destroys it, and behold, it is vanished"* (21:18).

Ibn Kathir highlights a second dimension of the same ayah: the sending down of revelation itself. He compares it to *"He sends the Revelation by His command to any of His servants He wills"* (40:15) — meaning He sends the angel to whomsoever He wills of His servants among the people on earth. So the ayah carries both senses the commentators bring out: the truth is *sent down* by Allah's choice, and it comes down *with force* upon falsehood.

**"The All-Knower of the Unseen" (*ʿAllām al-ghuyūb*).** Ibn Kathir: nothing whatsoever is hidden from Him in the heavens or on earth. This is the answer to any suspicion that the message is guesswork. It comes from the One from whom nothing is concealed — and He is the One choosing where to aim it.

## Ayah 49 — truth has come; falsehood cannot begin again

**"The truth has come, and falsehood can neither create anything nor resurrect."** Ibn Kathir: truth and the great Law have come from Allah, and falsehood has gone and has perished and vanished. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān presses the two verbs: falsehood becomes so incapacitated in the face of truth that **it can neither originate anything nor bring it back.** It cannot start, and it cannot restart. Its power to produce or reproduce is finished.

Ibn Kathir records a moment in which this ayah was recited aloud. When the Messenger of Allah ﷺ entered al-Masjid al-Ḥarām on the day of the conquest of Makkah and found those idols standing around the Kaʿbah, he started to hit the idols with his bow, reciting: *"And say: The truth has come and the falsehood has vanished. Surely, the falsehood is ever bound to vanish"* (17:81), and *"Say: The truth has come, and the falsehood can neither create anything nor resurrect."* This was recorded by Al-Bukhari, Muslim, At-Tirmidhi and An-Nasa'i.

The words Ibn Kathir glosses as *falsehood has gone and has perished and vanished* were, in that moment, being recited over the very objects they describe.

## Ayah 50 — where guidance comes from, and where error comes from

**"If I am astray, the loss is only mine. And if I am guided, it is by what my Lord reveals to me."** Ibn Kathir's summary: **all good comes from Allah**, and in what Allah sends down of revelation and clear truth there is guidance and wisdom; so whoever goes astray, does so by himself.

The humility here is total. The Prophet ﷺ claims no share in the guidance he brings — it is revelation — while any straying is charged to the one who strays. Ibn Kathir cites the same posture from ʿAbdullāh bin Masʿūd, may Allah be pleased with him, who said, when he was asked about some issue: **"I will say what I think, and if it is correct, then it is from Allah, and if it is wrong, then it is from me and from the Shayṭān, and Allah and His Messenger have nothing to do with it."**

**"Truly, He is All-Hearer, Ever Near" (*Samīʿ, Qarīb*).** Ibn Kathir explains: He hears all the words of His servants, and He is always near to respond to them when they call on Him.

Ibn Kathir cites here the ḥadīth of Abu Mūsā, which An-Nasa'i recorded and which also appears in the Two Ṣaḥīḥs: **"You are not calling upon one who is deaf or absent; you are calling upon One Who is All-Hearer, Ever Near and Responsive."**

## Living it

- **The one thing asked of the Quraysh is still the one thing asked of us.** Before examining a claim about Allah's religion, do the *qiyām lillāh*: start with a mind cleansed of previous thoughts and beliefs, seeking Allah's pleasure alone, so that old thoughts and deeds do not obstruct the way to accepting truth. Then reflect.
- **Both ways of thinking are open to you.** As Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ayah, you may think it out alone and in private, or consult friends and elders, discuss it and reach a conclusion — go by whichever of the two you like.
- **Remove suspicion from your own daʿwah.** Ayah 47's method is to hand back anything that could be mistaken for a fee, and to seek the reward with Allah, who knows both the message and the manner in which it is conveyed.
- **Echo Ibn Masʿūd's words.** If what you say is correct, it is from Allah; if it is wrong, it is from you and from the Shayṭān — and Allah and His Messenger ﷺ have nothing to do with it.
- **Call on Him knowing who hears.** Not the deaf, not the absent — the All-Hearer, the Ever Near, the Responsive.

passages.title: Belief offered too late, escape sealed off
passages.tafsir:
These four ayat close Sūrah Saba' with a single scene: the moment the deniers finally say "we believe" — and discover that the door through which faith is accepted has already shut behind them. What binds the passage together is one governing idea, drawn out in a series of contrasts between **near** and **far**: they are seized from a place *near*, but the faith they suddenly reach for lies at a place *far off*; in the world they threw their opinions about the Unseen from *far away*; and in the end a barrier is set between them and everything they wanted. Distance, in this passage, is the whole verdict.

## "If only you could see" — ayah 51

Ibn Kathir reads the opening as an address to the Prophet ﷺ: *if only you could see, O Muhammad, when these deniers are terrified on the Day of Resurrection, and they have no way of escape and nowhere to run to and no refuge.* The verse does not argue; it puts a scene in front of the eyes. The people who had been dismissing resurrection as a fantasy are shown to us at the very instant the fantasy turns out to be the ground under their feet.

**فَلَا فَوْتَ — "no escape."** Ibn Kathir closes three different exits in one breath: no way of escape, nowhere to run to, no refuge.

**"And they will be seized from a near place."** Ibn Kathir: *they will not even be given the slightest chance of escape, but they will be seized from the first instant.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān draws out the picture with a comparison from ordinary life: in this world, when a culprit runs, he has to be searched for; nothing of that kind happens here. All of them are simply seized from where they are located, and no one will have the chance to escape. What both commentators press on is the absence of any interval — no gap between the summons and the seizing, no moment in which to bolt.

**When does this happen?** Here the commentators genuinely differ, and the sources record the views side by side without resolving them. Most commentators, Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reports, take the seizing to belong to the Day of Resurrection (*al-hashr*), whose terror no disbeliever or sinner will be able to escape however hard he tries. Al-Hasan Al-Basri, cited by Ibn Kathir, identifies the near place with a moment: *"When they come forth from their graves."* Others, Maʿārif notes, take the time to be that of the agony of death — when the time of death comes they are terrified, unable to extricate themselves from the hands of the angels, and are seized where they are with the soul taken out. The sources leave these as distinct opinions; what each of them shares is the point the ayah is making, that at that moment there is nowhere left to run.

## Tanāwush: reaching for something out of reach — ayah 52

Then the confession comes: **وَقَالُوا آمَنَّا بِهِ** — "We do believe in it." Ibn Kathir explains what they mean: on the Day of Resurrection they will say *we believe in Allah and His angels, Books and Messengers.* It is, on its face, a complete profession of faith. He sets beside it another passage of the Qur'an in which the criminals hang their heads before their Lord and say, "Our Lord! We have now seen and heard, so send us back that we will do righteous good deeds. Verily, we now believe with certainty" (32:12). Faith that has *seen* is no longer the faith that was being asked for.

**The word تَّنَاوُش (tanāwush).** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān opens up the root sense: *tanāwush* means to pick something up by stretching out one's hand. And once you know that, the logic of the ayah is plain — one can pick up only what is near at hand; if it is very far, it will be out of reach. So the question **وَأَنَّىٰ لَهُمُ التَّنَاوُشُ مِن مَّكَانٍ بَعِيدٍ** — "how can they achieve it from a place so far off?" — states a simple impossibility. Mujahid glosses *tanāwush* with the plainest paraphrase: *"How could they attain that?"*

Why is it now out of reach? Ibn Kathir gives the reason in a line worth reading slowly: they are *"so far removed from the place where it could be accepted from them, and they have entered the realm of the Hereafter which is the realm of reward and punishment, not the realm of trial and testing."* Had they believed in this world, that would have been good for them; but having entered the Hereafter, there is no way their faith can be accepted — *just as there is no way a person can get a thing if he is far away from it.* Maʿārif ul Qurʼān makes the same point in its own terms: *īmān* (faith) is a thing of the life of this mortal world, and that alone is what is accepted; the Ākhirah is not *dār al-ʿamal*, the venue of deeds, the place to act rightly. Nothing done there can be taken into account. How, then, could they pick up the great wealth of *īmān* simply by stretching out a hand for it?

Two of the early authorities put the pathos of it exactly. Az-Zuhri: *"They will wish to attain faith when they have reached the Hereafter and are cut off from this world."* Al-Hasan Al-Basri: *"They will seek something when they have no way of attaining it, they will seek faith from a distant place."*

Notice how the two "places" of ayat 51 and 52 work against each other. For the seizing, everything is *near* — they are taken from where they stand, in the first instant. For faith, everything is suddenly *far* — the one thing they now want stands at a distance no stretch of the hand can cross. The same person, in the same moment, is too close to escape and too far to reach.

## Arrows shot in the dark — ayah 53

Ayah 53 keeps that same measure of distance and turns it backwards, onto what these people were doing while faith was still near at hand. Ibn Kathir: *how can they attain faith in the Hereafter when in this world they disbelieved in the truth and denied the Messengers?*

**وَيَقْذِفُونَ بِالْغَيْبِ — "and they used to conjecture about the Unseen."** Malik narrated from Zayd bin Aslam that this means *"by guessing,"* the same idea Allah expresses elsewhere as **رَجْمًا بِالْغَيْبِ**, "guessing at the Unseen" (18:22). Maʿārif ul Qurʼān unpacks the verb: *qadhf* means to hit something by throwing. In Arab idiom, anyone talking with no proof for what he says is described with exactly these two expressions — *rajm bi'l-ghayb* and *qadhf bi'l-ghayb* — because such a person shoots arrows in the dark, with no aim or target. That is the image: confident-sounding statements about matters no one can see, launched at nothing.

Ibn Kathir shows what those arrows actually were. About the Prophet ﷺ: *sometimes they said he was a poet, sometimes they said he was a soothsayer, or a sorcerer, or a mad man, or other baseless comments.* Read the charges in a row and their inconsistency is itself part of the point — this is the sound of guessing, not of knowing. And about the resurrection they said, as Allah quotes them, "we do not think it but as a conjecture, and we have no firm convincing belief" (45:32). Qatadah and Mujahid comment: *"Their belief that there would be no resurrection, no Paradise and no Hell was based on mere conjecture."* They were not certain there was nothing after death; they were guessing that there was nothing — and staking everything on the guess.

**"From a far place."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives a striking reading of these words here: what they say is *far from their hearts* — that is, they do not believe it in their hearts. On this reading the phrase measures a second distance. In ayah 52 what they want is far from them; here what they say is far from them. Their claims had no support in the reality outside them, and no conviction inside them either.

## The barrier — ayah 54

**وَحِيلَ بَيْنَهُمْ وَبَيْنَ مَا يَشْتَهُونَ** — "and a barrier will be set between them and that which they desire." This is where the passage's distances harden into something built. The wording does not name the thing desired, and the early commentators fill it in differently:

- **Faith** — Al-Hasan Al-Basri, Ad-Dahhak and others.
- **Repentance** — As-Suddi, and this was also the view of Ibn Jarir.
- **This world and its wealth, luxuries and people** — Mujahid; something similar was narrated from Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas and Ar-Rabi' bin Anas, and Ibn Kathir notes it is also the opinion of Al-Bukhari and the Group.

Here — unlike the difference over timing in ayah 51 — Ibn Kathir explicitly reconciles the readings himself: *"The correct view is that there is no contradiction between the two views, for a barrier will be set between them and what they desire in this world, and what they seek in the Hereafter will be denied from them."* Both losses land on the same person. Everything he spent his life wanting is walled off from him, and the one thing he now wants — faith, repentance — is refused. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān reads the ayah along both of those lines too: it could be true of the Day of Judgment, in the sense that these people will be seeking salvation and Paradise but fail to have it; and it could apply to the time of death in the world, in that the worldly wealth they wished to have was made to stay away from them by the barrier of death.

**كَمَا فُعِلَ بِأَشْيَاعِهِم — "as was done in the past with the people of their kind."** Maʿārif ul Qurʼān explains that *ashyāʿ* is the plural of *shīʿah*: one who is a follower of someone and thinks alike is called a *shīʿah*, a partisan of that person. The word gathers these deniers into a long line of people who took the same position and received the same answer. Ibn Kathir names what that answer was: this happened *"to the nations of the past who disbelieved in the Messengers; when the punishment of Allah came upon them, they wished that they had believed, but this was not accepted from them."* He cites the passage where Allah states the rule outright: "So, when they saw Our punishment, they said: 'We believe in Allah Alone and reject all that we used to associate with Him as partners.' Then their faith could not avail them when they saw Our punishment. Like this has been the way of Allah in dealing with His servants. And there the disbelievers lost utterly" (40:84–85). *Sunnat Allāh* — the way of Allah with His servants. This is not an arbitrary refusal but a settled order: belief that arrives only once the punishment is in view is not the belief that was ever being asked for.

## "In grave doubt" — the last words of the sūrah

**إِنَّهُمْ كَانُوا فِي شَكٍّ مُرِيبٍ** — "Verily, they have been in grave doubt." Ibn Kathir explains the connection: *in this world they had doubts, so their faith will not be accepted from them when they behold the punishment with their own eyes.* The doubt was the disease; the useless confession at the end is only its final symptom. Maʿārif ul Qurʼān specifies the content of that doubt, and with it names the reason for everything the passage has described: they did not believe in the prophethood of Sayyidnā Muhammad al-Mustafā ﷺ, nor did they have the certitude of and faith in the Qur'an being the Divine word.

Ibn Kathir closes his commentary on Sūrah Saba' by quoting Qatadah, and it is hard to imagine a better last word on the passage: *"Beware of doubt. For whoever dies doubting, will be raised doubting; and whoever dies believing, with certainty will be raised believing with certainty."*

## Living it

Read as a whole, these four ayat are not really about them. They are about the shape of the opportunity you are in — and about which things, in your life right now, are near and which are far.

**Faith is a *now* thing, and only a now thing.** On Ibn Kathir's reading, this world is the realm of trial and testing and the next is the realm of reward and punishment; Maʿārif ul Qurʼān adds that the Hereafter is not the venue of deeds and nothing done there can be taken into account. Faith is near at hand while you are here. Nothing you postpone until you can *see* will be worth anything when you can.

**Do not build on a guess.** The people of ayah 53 were not confident men with an argument; on the reading Maʿārif ul Qurʼān gives, they were shooting arrows in the dark, with no aim or target. Every generation has its own version of the claim that there is no resurrection, no Paradise and no Hell — and, as Qatadah and Mujahid observed of the first generation to make it, that claim rests on mere conjecture.

**Qatadah's warning is directed at the living.** A person is raised in the state he dies in — so doubt is not something to leave for later, because later is precisely the place where, as ayah 52 has just shown, faith is no longer within reach. And if you have not put your desires where they belong, the barrier of ayah 54 comes for the whole arrangement at once: everything you wanted walled off, and the thing you finally want refused. That refusal is not cruelty. It is simply what it means that this life, and not the next, was the place where the hand could still reach.
